1:4.annotated: Master[1] of the Day of Recompense.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem, Al-Kesa’i, Yaʻqub and Khalaf in one of his narrations read it as: “King of the Day of Recompense.”

2:2.annotated: That is the Scripture; there is no doubt about it—a guidance for the mindful(of God) ,[1]

footnotes.text: This portion can be read differently in Arabic by pausing after ‘doubt’, and in this case it means: ‘That is the Scripture, no doubt. In it there is guidance for the mindful (of God).’

2:7.annotated: Allah has set a seal on their hearts and on their hearing, and over their sight(s )[1]is a veil; for for them is a great punishment.

footnotes.text: Mentioned in plural form in Arabic, denoted by (s) in English for grammatical reasons.

2:9.annotated: They try to deceive Allah and those who have attained faith, yet they deceive[1] none but themselves, but they are unaware.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . yet they try to deceive none but . . .”

2:10.annotated: In their hearts is sickness, so Allah increased their sickness, and for them is a painful punishment on account of how they used to lie[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . they used to disbelieve .”

2:17.annotated: Their likeness is that of a person who kindled a fire, but when it illuminated all around him, Allah took away their[1]light and left them in darkness(es) [2], unable to see.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.
Mentioned in plural form in Arabic, denoted by (es) in English for grammatical reasons.

2:23.annotated: And if you<sup>pl </sup>are in doubt about what We have bestowed upon Our servant from on high, then bring a single surah[1]of its like, and call your witnesses apart from Allah if you are truthful.

footnotes.text: Each portion of the Qur’an is called a ‘surah’, which is sometimes translated as ‘chapter’.

2:24.annotated: But if you<sup>pl </sup>do not—and you will not—then be mindful of the Fire[1]whose fuel is people and stones; it has been prepared for the deniers.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘protect yourselves against the Fire’.

2:28.annotated: How can you<sup>pl </sup>deny Allah when you were lifeless and He gave you life, then He puts you to death, then He brings you to life, then to Him you are returned[1] ?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . to Him you return ?”

2:29.annotated: It is He Who created for you<sup>pl </sup>what is on earth, all together, then turned to the heaven and formed them[1]into seven heavens. And He is All-Knowing of everything.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:34.annotated: And recall when We said to the angels, “Prostrate yourselves to Adam”, so they prostrated themselves—but not Iblis[1]. He refused and acted arrogantly and became of the deniers.

footnotes.text: Iblis is another name of Satan or Shaytan.

2:36.annotated: Yet Satan made them slip[1] therefrom, so he brought them out of what they were in. Then We said, “Descend<sup>pl </sup>, as enemies to one another, for in the earth you<sup>pl </sup>have a place of settlement and enjoyment for a while.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “Yet Satan removed them therefrom . . .”

2:37.annotated: Thereupon Adam received words[1] from his Lord. Thus, He granted him repentance and accepted it from him. Indeed, it is He Who is the Superb Granter and Accepter of repentance, the Bestower of mercy.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “Thereupon Adam was received by words from His Lord.”

2:38.annotated: We said, “Descend from it, all together. Then whenever any guidance comes to you from Me, then whoever follows My guidance—then no fear[1] shall beupon them[2]nor shall they grieve.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . then no fear shall ever be upon them nor shall they grieve.”
A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:41.annotated: And believe<sup>pl </sup>in what I have sent down, confirming what is with you<sup>pl </sup>. And do not be the first denier[1]of it, and do not purchase, inexchange for My revelations, a small price, and be mindful of Me alone.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from plural to singular.

2:43.annotated: And establish the prayer, and bring[1]the purifying charity[2], and bow down with the ones bowing down.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

2:48.annotated: And be mindful of a day[1]when no self avails another in anything, nor is any intercession accepted on its behalf, nor is any ransom taken from it, nor are they<sup>d </sup> supported.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘protect yourselves against a day’.

2:49.annotated: And recall how We delivered you<sup>pl </sup>from Pharaoh’s folk—(those) inflicting[1]upon you an evil punishment, slaying your sons and keeping your women alive(in bondage) . For therein is a great test from your Lord.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift describing past events in present tense, serving to create a vivid portrait of events.

2:51.annotated: And recall when We appointed with[1] Moses forty nights. Then you<sup>pl </sup>took the calf(for worship) after him, while you were unjust.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . appointed for Moses . . .”

2:54.annotated: And recall when Moses said to his people, “O my people, you have done injustice to yourselves by taking the calf(for worship) . So repent to your Maker and kill yourselves[1]. That would be better for you with your Maker.” So He granted you repentance and accepted it from you; indeed it is He who is the Superb Granter and Accepter of repentance, the Bestower of mercy.

footnotes.text: By mortifying it.

2:58.annotated: And recall when We said, “Enter this town and eat from it freely wherever you<sup>pl </sup>will, but enter the gate bowing down and say, ‘disburden(us) ’. We(will)forgive you your offenses[1] , and We will give more to those who excel in doing good.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “Your offenses will be forgiven for you . . .”

2:61.annotated: And recall when you<sup>pl </sup>said, “O Moses, we shall not endure one kind of food, so call upon your Lord to bring out for us of what the earth germinates: of its herbs and its cucumbers and its garlic and its lentils and its onions.” He said, “Would you<sup>pl </sup>exchange what is better for what is less? Go down to Egypt where you will have what you asked for.” And they[1]were struck with humiliation and destituteness, and they incurred wrath from Allah. That was because they used to deny Allah’s signs[2]and unjustifiably kill the prophets. That was because they disobeyed and used to transgress.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 2<sup>nd </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

2:62.annotated: Indeed, those who have attained faith and those who have Judaized and the Christians and the Sabians—whoever has attained faith in Allah and the Last Day and has acted righteously—then their[1]reward is with their Lord, and no fear[2] shall beupon them nor shall they grieve.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.
Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and no fear shall ever be upon them nor shall they grieve.”

2:74.annotated: Then after that your hearts hardened, so that they were as rocks or even harder. For surely from some rocks rivers gush out, and surely some others splinter so that water comes out from them, and surely some others sink in awe of Allah. And Allah is never oblivious of what you[1] do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “. . . of what they do .”

2:78.annotated: And among them[1]are illiterates who do not know the Scripture, other than fancies, and they only speculate.

footnotes.text: The Jews.

2:79.annotated: So woe to those who scribe the Scripture with their own hands and then say, “This is from Allah,” that they may purchase, in exchange for it, a small price. Woe to them on account of what their hands have written, and woe to them on account of what they earn[1].

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from past tense to present tense.

2:81.annotated: Yes indeed, whoever has earned an evil deed and whose offense has[1] surrounded him—then those are the fellows of the Fire; therein they abide.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . whose offenses have surrounded . . .”

2:83.annotated: And recall when We took a pledge from the Children of Israel: “You[1] shall worshipnone but Allah, and excel in showing kindness to the parents and the relative and orphans and the destitute<sup>pl </sup>, and say kind words to mankind and establish the prayers and bring[2]the purifying charity[3].” Then you[4]turned away in disregard, except for a few of you.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Hamza and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “They shall worship . . .”
The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.
A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 2<sup>nd </sup>person.

2:85.annotated: Then here you are, killing yourselves and evicting a group of your own from their homes—backing each other against them in sin and hostility. And if they come to you as captives, you do ransom[1] them, while their eviction is forbidden to you. Is it that you believe in part of the Scripture and deny part? So what is the repayment for those of you who do that but disgrace in the Earlier Life, and(that) on the Day of Resurrection they are turned back to the most severe punishment? For Allah is never oblivious of what you[2] do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ, ʻAsem, Al-Kesa’i, Yaʻqub and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . you ransom them,”
Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Shuʻbah, Yaʻqub and Khalaf in his preferred narration read it as: “. . . what they do .”

2:87.annotated: And most surely, We brought Moses the Scripture and sent a succession of messengers after him. And We brought Jesus, son of Mary, the evident proofs, and We aided him with the Holy Spirit. Is it that every time a messenger came to you with anything your(inner) selves do not desire, you acted arrogantly, so one group you disbelieved, and another group you kill[1]?

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from past tense to present tense; using present tense for an old practice emphasizes that it was a tradition frequently practiced.

2:90.annotated: Miserable is what they have purchased in exchange for their(very) selves—that they deny what Allah has bestowed from on high[1] , out of resentment that Allah would send down His grace upon whomever He wills of His servants. Thus they incurred wrath upon wrath, for for the deniers is a demeaning punishment.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . what Allah has sent down . . .”

2:91.annotated: And when it is said to them, “Believe in what Allah has sent down,” they say, “We believe in what was sent down to us,” and they deny anything beyond that, although it is the truth which confirms what they have. Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Why(then) do you kill[1]Allah’s prophets—earlier—if you are believers?”

footnotes.text: Using present tense for an old practice emphasizes that it was a tradition frequently practiced.

2:96.annotated: And you<sup>sg </sup>will most surely find them the most adhering of mankind to life, and more so than those who associated(others with God) . Every one of them would love to have his life extended a thousand years, but being granted a long life does not nudge him from the punishment, for Allah is All-Seeing of what they[1] do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . of what you <sup>pl </sup>do .”

2:97.annotated: Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel…[1]—for indeed, it is he who has bestowed it upon your<sup>sg </sup>heart from on high by Allah’s leave, confirming what preceded it, and guidance and glad tidings for the believers.”

footnotes.text: This sentence is left open-ended; according to Ibn ʻAshour and other exegetes, its predicate is “then let him take God as an enemy.”

2:102.annotated: and they followed what the devils read[1]during the reign of Solomon. But never did Solomon deny[2]; rather it was the Satans who denied, teaching people sorcery and what was sent down in Babylon to the two angels Harut and Marut. And they do not teach anybody until they say, “We are but a means of trial, so do not deny(faith) .” Even so, they learn from them the means to cause separation between a man and his spouse—but never could they harm anyone except by Allah’s leave. And they learn what would harm them and not benefit them. Yet they did know that whoever purchased it[3]would have no share in the Hereafter. So indeed, how miserable is what they sold themselves for, if they only knew!

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from past tense to present tense; using present tense for an old practice emphasizes that it was a tradition frequently practiced.
Blaspheme.
Sorcery.

2:104.annotated: O you who have attained faith, do not say ‘Raʻina,’[1]but say, ‘Unthurna,’[2]and listen, for for the deniers is a painful punishment.

footnotes.text: This word means ‘Pay heed to us’ but sounds similar to a Hebrew word that means ‘the most evil of us’.
Grant us consideration.

2:105.annotated: Neither the deniers from among the People of the Scripture nor the polytheists would love that any good be sent down upon you[1] fromyour<sup>pl </sup>Lord. Yet Allah specifies for His mercy whomever He wills, for Allah is the Possessor of great grace.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . be bestowed upon you from on high by your<sup>pl </sup>Lord.”

2:106.annotated: Never do We abrogate[1] any sign[2]nor cause it to be forgotten[3] unless We bring one better than it or similar to it. Have you<sup>sg </sup>not come to know that Allah is All-Powerful over everything?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “Never do we command the abrogation of any . . .”

The Arabic word used isayah. Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . nor postpone it unless We . . .”

2:110.annotated: And establish the prayer and bring[1]the purifying charity[2], for whatever good you forward for yourselves, you will find it with Allah. Indeed, Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

2:112.annotated: Yes indeed, whoever submits his face(in worship) to Allah while excelling in doing good, then he has his reward with his Lord, and no fear[1] shall beupon them[2]nor shall they grieve.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and no fear shall ever be upon them nor shall they grieve.”
A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:116.annotated: And they[1] said, “Allah has taken(for Himself) offspring.” Highly Exalted is He. Rather, to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth; all are devout towards Him—

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “They said . . .”

2:117.annotated: the Innovator of the heavens and the earth, and whenever He decrees a matter, He only says to it, “Be,” and so it is[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “He only says to it, ‘Be,’ so it is.”

2:119.annotated: We have indeed sent you with the truth as a herald of glad tidings and as a warner, for you will not be asked[1] about the fellows of purgatory.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . as a warner, so do not ask about the fellows of purgatory.”

2:121.annotated: Those to whom We have brought the Scripture read it as it ought to be read; those ones believe in it. But whoever denies it—then those[1]are the losers.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:123.annotated: And be<sup>pl </sup>mindful of a day[1]when no self avails any other self in anything, nor is any ransom accepted from it, nor does any intercession benefit it, nor are they<sup>b </sup> supported.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘protect yourselves against a day’.

2:124.annotated: And recall when Abraham[1] was tried by his Lord with certain words and he fulfilled them. He said, “I am appointing you as a leader for mankind.” He said, “And of my offspring?” He said, “My covenant does not include the unjust<sup>pl </sup>.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham and Ibn Zekwan in one of his narrations read it as: “Abraham ”.

2:125.annotated: And recall when We made the House a resort for mankind, and a sanctuary.And[1] take<sup>pl </sup>from Abraham’s<sup>e </sup>standing place a place of prayer. And We covenanted with Abraham and Ishmael, “Cleanse My House for circumambulators and consecrators and those bowing down and prostrating themselves.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ and Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “And they took from Abraham’s . . .”

2:128.annotated: Our Lord, and make us both Muslim[1]to You, and from our offspring a Muslim community(submitting) to You. And show us our rites, and grant us repentance and accept it from us; indeed, it is You, You(alone) who are the Superb Granter and Accepter of repentance, the Bestower of mercy.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Muslimayn, the dual form ofMuslimeenwhich means those who willingly submit to God, regardless of which prophet they followed.

2:129.annotated: Our Lord, and send forth among them a messenger from themselves to read to them Your signs[1]and teach them the Scripture and the wisdom and purify them. Indeed, it is you, You(alone) , who are the Almighty, the All-Wise.”

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is ayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

2:130.annotated: And who would forsake the creed of Abraham[1] except he who fools himself? And We have indeed chosen him in the Earlier(Life) , and in the Hereafter he is most surely one of the righteous.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham and Ibn Zekwan in one of his narrations read it as: “Abraham ”.

2:132.annotated: And with this Abraham<sup>b </sup>frequentlyenjoined[1] his children, and(so did) Jacob, “O my children, Allah has indeed chosen the religion for you, so do not die except as Muslims[2].”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “And with this Abrahamenjoined . . .”
The Arabic word used is Muslimoonwhich means those who willingly submit to God, regardless of which prophet they followed.

2:140.annotated: Or do you[1] say<sup>pl </sup>that Abraham[2] and Ishmael and Isaac and Jacob and the Grandsons[3]were Jews or Christians? Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Do you know better or Allah?” And who is more unjust than one who conceals a testimony he has from Allah? For Allahis not oblivious of what you<sup>pl </sup>do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Abu Jaʻfar, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Shuʻba and Rouh read it as: “Or do they say . . .”
Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham and Ibn Zekwan in one of his narrations read it as: “Abraham ”.
The sons of Jacob.

2:143.annotated: And thus have We made you a middle community, that you may be witnesses over humanity and that the Messenger may be a witness over you. Thus We only assigned the direction of prayer, which you formerly followed, that We may distinguish the one who follows the Messenger from the one who turns on his heels. And it was indeed difficult, except for those whom Allah has guided. But never would Allah let your faith[1]go to waste; indeed, towards mankind, Allah has always been truly Compassionate, Bestowing of mercy.

footnotes.text: It means ‘your prayers performed towards the former direction’.

2:144.annotated: We have surely seen the turning about of your<sup>sg </sup>face towards the heaven. So We will turn you towards a direction that pleases you. So turn your face towards the Inviolable Mosque. And wherever you<sup>pl </sup>may be, turn your faces[1]towards it. Indeed, those who were brought the Scripture know that it is the truth from their Lord. And Allah is not oblivious of what they[2] do.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.
Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i, Abu Jaʻfar and Rouh read it as: “. . . of what you <sup>pl </sup>do .”

2:146.annotated: Those whom We have brought the Scripture recognize him[1]as they recognize their own children. But indeed a group of them do conceal the truth while they know.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 2<sup>nd </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

2:148.annotated: Thus for each is a direction towards which he turns[1] , so race<sup>pl </sup>towards good works. Wherever you may be, Allah will bring you all together. Allah is indeed Powerful over everything.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . towards which he is turned .”

2:149.annotated: And from wherever you<sup>sg </sup>set out, turn your face towards the Inviolable Mosque, for this is indeed the truth from your Lord. And Allah is not oblivious of what you[1] do<sup>pl </sup>.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . of what they do .”

2:151.annotated: Just as We sent among you a messenger from yourselves, reading Our signs[1]to you, and purifying you, and teaching you the Scripture and wisdom, and teaching you what you did not know.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

2:154.annotated: And do not say<sup>pl </sup>of anyone who is killed in the way of Allah, “(They are) dead[1].” Rather,(they are) alive, but you are unaware.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:158.annotated: Indeed, Al-Safa and Al-Marwa are among the rites of Allah, so whoever performs Pilgrimage[1]to the House or performs Minor Pilgrimage[2], then no sin is committed by him if he circumambulates them. And whoever volunteers a good act—then Allah is indeed Thankful, All-Knowing.

footnotes.text: Hajj.
Umrah.

2:164.annotated: Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of the night and the day, and the ships that sail the sea with what benefits mankind, and the water that Allah sent down from the sky— with which He revived the earth after it had died and scattered in it all kinds of treading creatures, and the shifting of the winds[1] , and the clouds disposed between the sky and the earth are surely signs for people who reason.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “wind ”.

2:165.annotated: Yet of mankind is one who takes(others) apart from Allah as rivals to Him. They[1]love them with a love like that due to Allah, yet those who have attained faith are stronger in love for Allah. And if only those who have done injustice could see[2] , when they see[3] the punishment, that[4] all power belongs to Allah and thatAllah is severe in punishment.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.
Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Yaʻqub read it as: “And if only you <sup>sg </sup>could see those who have done injustice . . .”
Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . when they are made to see the punishment . . .”
Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . could see, when they seethe punishment: indeed all power belongs to Allah and indeed Allah is . . .”

2:166.annotated: Recall when those who were followed disowned[1]those who had followed(them) , and they saw the punishment and ties between them were severed.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

2:167.annotated: And those who followed said, “If only we could have another chance so we could disown them as they disowned us.” Thus Allah shows[1]them their deeds as regrets to them, and never will they come out of the Fire.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from past tense to present tense.

2:171.annotated: The parable of those who have denied is that of one[1]who hollers out to things that hear nothing but mere calls and cries. Deaf, dumb,(and) blind, so they do not reason.

footnotes.text: A shepherd.

2:172.annotated: O you who have attained faith, eat of the good things We have provided you, and give thanks to Allah[1]if it is He that you worship.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

2:177.annotated: Virtue is not(attained) by turning your<sup>pl </sup>faces towards the East and the West. Rather, virtue is(exemplified) in one who has attained faith in Allah and the Last Day and the angels and the Scripture and the prophets, and has brought money—despite his love of it—to relatives and orphans and the destitute<sup>pl </sup>and the traveler in need and the askers and for(the freeing of) slaves[1], and has established the prayer and brought[2]the purifying charity[3]; and(it is exemplified) in those[4]who fulfill their covenant when they have covenanted, and those who are patient in(the face of) misery and adversity and at the time of battle. Those are the ones who were truthful, and it is those who are the mindful(of God) .

footnotes.text: Literally ‘necks’.
The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.
A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:181.annotated: But whoever changes it[1]after he has heard it, then surely its sin is upon those who change it. Indeed, Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.

footnotes.text: The will.

2:184.annotated: (This fasting is for) a limited number of days. But should any one of you be sick or on a journey, then(he should fast) a period of other days. Yet for those who can fast with difficulty[1], a compensation(is allowed instead)—food for a destitute person[2] . But whoever volunteers a good act, it is better for him. Yet to fast is better for you<sup>pl </sup>, if you only knew.

footnotes.text: This sign was revealed at a time when fasting was not yet obligatory, then it was abrogated by sign 185.

Qira’at: Hisham read it as: “a compensation (is allowed instead)—food for destitute people .” Nafieʻ, Ibn Zekwan and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . a compensation of food for destitute persons (is allowed instead .)”

2:185.annotated: (It was) the month of Ramadan in which the Recital[1]was sent down as guidance for mankind, and as evident explanations of the guidance and the criterion. So whoever of you witnesses the month, then he shall fast it. But whoever is sick or on a journey, then(he must fast) a period of other days. Allah wants ease for you and does not want hardship for you, and that you should complete the period, and that you should glorify Allah for having guided you, and so that you may give thanks.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’an which literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

2:188.annotated: And do not devour your wealths among yourselves by false means, nor throw it(as bribes) to the judges in order to devour part[1]of other people’s wealth illicitly, while you know.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘a group’.

2:189.annotated: They ask you<sup>sg </sup>about the crescents. Say, “They are time-marks for mankind and for the Pilgrimage[1].” And virtue is not(attained) by approaching houses from their backs; rather, virtue is(exemplified in) one who has been mindful(of God) . So approach houses from their doors[2]and be mindful of Allah, that you<sup>pl </sup>may succeed.

footnotes.text: Hajj.

Before Islam, Arabs used to enter their houses through the backyards once they had donned their Hajj garments, thinking that entering through the door would invalidate their state of consecration for pilgrimage.

2:191.annotated: And kill them wherever you<sup>pl </sup>encounter them, and evict them from where they have evicted you, for religious persecution is more severe than killing. But do not combat[1] them at the Inviolable Mosque unless they combatyou about it. So if they combatyou<sup>pl </sup>, then kill them. Such is the repayment of the deniers.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “But do not kill them at the Inviolable Mosque unless they kill you about it. So if they kill you<sup>pl </sup>, then kill them.”

2:196.annotated: And complete the Pilgrimage[1]and the Minor Pilgrimage[2]for Allah. But if you<sup>pl </sup>are detained, then(offer) whatever is feasible of offerings. And do not shave your heads until the offering has reached its destination. But whoever of you is sick or has some affliction of his head, then the due redemption is fasting or a donation or a sacrifice. Then when you are secure: whoever enjoys a break between the Minor Pilgrimage and the Pilgrimage, then(he must offer) whatever is feasible of offering. But whoever cannot find the means, then fasting for three days during the Pilgrimage, and seven when you<sup>pl </sup>have[3]returned; that is ten in total. That is for the one whose family is not present at the Inviolable Mosque[4]. And be<sup>pl </sup>mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is stern in retribution.

footnotes.text: Hajj.
Umrah.
A grammatical shift from singular to plural.
Lives outside Makkah.

2:197.annotated: Pilgrimage is during specific months. So whoever decides to perform Pilgrimage, then there shall never be intercourse nor ungodliness nor disputation[1] during the Pilgrimage. And whatever good you<sup>pl </sup>do, Allah knows it. And take provisions, but the best provision is indeed mindfulness(of God) . And be mindful of Me[2], O people of understanding.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . then there shall be no intercourse nor ungodliness nor disputation during the Pilgrimage.”Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . then there shall be no intercourse nor ungodliness, and no disputation, ever, during the Pilgrimage.”
A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

2:198.annotated: You<sup>pl </sup>commit no sin[1] by seeking grace from your Lord[2]. So when you<sup>pl </sup>pour forth from Arafat, remember Allah at the Sacred Landmark. And remember Him as He has guided you<sup>pl </sup>, although before that, you were indeed of those astray.

footnotes.text: During Pilgrimage.
Through commerce.

2:203.annotated: And remember<sup>pl </sup>Allah[1]during a limited number of days. But whoever hurries on(to leave Mena) after two days commits no sin, and whoever stays on commits no sin—provided he maintains mindfulness(of God) . And be<sup>pl </sup>mindful of Allah, and know that to Him you will be herded.

footnotes.text: In the valley of Mena.

2:210.annotated: Are they waiting for anything except for(the command of) Allah to come to them in shades of mists, and the angels(too)[1]? And(thus) the matter was[2]settled, for to Allah all things are returned[3] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . in shades of mists and angels ?”
A grammatical shift from present tense to past tense.
All except for Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, ʻAsem and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . all things return .”

2:213.annotated: Mankind used to be one community, then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of glad tidings and as forewarners. And He sent down with them the Scripture with the truth to judge[1] between mankind regarding whatever they differed over. But none differed over it[2]except those who were given it—after evident proofs had come to them—out of mutual envy between them. Then Allah guided those who attained faith to the truth they had disputed, by His knowledge[3]. For Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . so that it may be judged between mankind . . .”
The Scripture.
Literally ‘by His leave’.

2:214.annotated: Or did you<sup>pl </sup>expect to enter the Garden(of Paradise) before the like of(the trials that befell) those who passed on before you had befallen you? Misery and adversity afflicted them, and they were shaken as with an earthquake, until[1] the Messenger and those who believed with him would say, “When is Allah’s support(coming) ?” Undoubtedly, Allah’s support is indeed near.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ read it as: “. . . and they were shaken as with an earthquake, such that the Messenger and those . . .”

2:217.annotated: They ask you<sup>sg </sup>about the inviolable month—(about) combat during it. Say, “Combat during it is(a) grave(offense) , yet barring(others) from the way of Allah and denying Him and(preventing access to) the Inviolable Mosque as well as evicting its people from it are graver to Allah, for religious persecution is(a) graver(offense) than killing. And they will keep combating you<sup>pl </sup>to turn you back from your religion, if they can. And whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies as a denier—those[1]are the ones whose deeds were nullified in the Earlier(Life) and the Hereafter, for those are the fellows of the Fire; therein they abide.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:219.annotated: They ask you<sup>sg </sup>about wine and gambling. Say, “There is grave sin[1] in them and some benefits for people, but the sin in them[2]is greater than their benefit.” And they ask you about what they should spend. Say, “The surplus.” Thus Allah makes the sign evident to you<sup>pl </sup>, that you may reflect

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “There is much sin in them . . .”
Literally ‘their sin’.

2:222.annotated: And they ask you<sup>sg </sup>about menstruation. Say, “It is(a cause of) harm, so keep<sup>pl </sup>away from(sexual intercourse with) women during menstruation, and do not approach them until they areclean[1] . But once they have cleansed themselves, then approach them from where Allah has commanded you.” Indeed, Allah loves those who frequently repent, and He loves those who cleanse themselves.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . until they are cleansed .”

2:229.annotated: Divorce is(allowed) twice, then either retention in accordance with what is fair, or setting free kindly. And it is not lawful for you<sup>pl </sup>to take back anything you have given them[1], unless they[2] both fear[3] that theymay not maintain Allah’s limits. So if you<sup>pl </sup>fear that they may not maintain Allah’s limits, then there is no sin committed by either of them if she pays, as a compensation for her release[4]. These are Allah’s limits, so do<sup>pl </sup>not transgress them, for those who transgress Allah’s limits are the unjust.

footnotes.text: ‘Them’ is feminine, denoting that the discourse is addressing men regarding their wives.
A grammatical shift from 2<sup>nd </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
Qira’at: Hamza, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . unless it is feared that they both may not maintain . . .”
Literally ‘ransoms herself’.

2:230.annotated: But if he divorces her, she shall not be lawful for him again until she has married another spouse. Then if he[1] divorces her, then no sin is committed by them both[2]if they reunite, provided they think they can maintain Allah’s limits. Thus these are Allah’s limits; He makes them evident to people who know.

footnotes.text: The latter.
She and the first husband.

2:231.annotated: Thus if you<sup>pl </sup>divorce women and they have reached their term[1], then either retain them in accordance with what is fair or release them in accordance with what is fair. But do not retain them in order to transgress against them, for whoever performs that, then he has surely been unjust to himself. And do not take Allah’s signs for mockery. And remember Allah’s blessing upon you<sup>pl </sup>and what He has sent down to you of the Scripture and the Wisdom to admonish you. And be<sup>pl </sup>mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is All-Aware of everything.

footnotes.text: The waiting period.

2:233.annotated: And mothers shall nurse their children for two whole years[1]—for whoever wants to complete the nursing period. And it is the duty of the father of the infant to provide for them[2]and clothe them in accordance with what is fair. No self shall be tasked beyond its capacity. No mother should be[3] harmed on account of her child, nor any father of an infant on account of his child. And the same duty rests upon the heir. And if they both want weaning, by mutual consent and consultation, then no sin is committed by them. And if you<sup>pl </sup>want[4]to seek nursing for your children, then no sin is committed by you as long as you give(them) what you have brought[5] in accordance with what is fair. And be mindful of Allah, and know that Allah is indeed All-Seeing of what you do.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘two rounds’.
The mothers.
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “No mother is (supposed to be) harmed on account of her child . . .”
A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 2<sup>nd </sup>person.
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “. . . what you<sup>pl </sup>have come up with . . .”

2:234.annotated: And those of you who are taken at death and leave spouses behind, they[1]shall keep themselves in wait for four months and ten days. Then when they have reached their term, then no sin is committed by you<sup>pl </sup>regarding what they might do with themselves in accordance with what is fair. For Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

footnotes.text: The pronoun is plural feminine, denoting that it means ‘the widows’.

2:235.annotated: And no sin is committed by you<sup>pl </sup>if you give a hint about engagement to(the widowed) women or if you keep it within yourselves. Allah already knew that you would consider(marrying) them[1]. But do not meet them secretly unless you have something to say in accordance with what is fair. And do not confirm the marriage tie until the term prescribed is fulfilled. And know that Allah knows what is in your(inner) selves, so beware of Him. And know that Allah is Oft-Forgiving, Forbearing.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘mention them’.

2:236.annotated: No sin is committed by you<sup>pl </sup>if you divorce women before having touched[1] them[2] nor appointed to them any marriage obligation[3]. And compensate them: the wealthy according to his means, and the poor according to his means—a compensation in accordance with what is fair, a duty upon those who excel in doing good.

footnotes.text: In sexual intercourse.
Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . before having touched each other . . .”
Dowry.

2:240.annotated: Moreover, those of you(men) who are taken at death and leave spouses behind—(let them bequeath)a bequest[1] for their spouses with compensation for a year without eviction(from the husband’s residence) . But if they depart, then no sin is committed by you<sup>pl </sup>regarding what they have done with themselves in accordance with what is fair. For Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer, Hafs and Hamza read it as: “. . . and leave spouses behind—a bequest (is ordained upon them) for their spouses with compensation . . .”

2:245.annotated: Who is it that will lend Allah a good loan?(So)that He may multiply it for him manifold[1] , forAllah withholds and extends, and to Him you<sup>pl </sup>are returned[2] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem, Ibn ʻAmer and Yaʻqub read it as: “Who is it that will lend Allah a good loan (so) that He may multiply it for him manifold? For Allah withholds and extends . . .”
Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . you <sup>pl </sup>return .”

2:247.annotated: Thus their prophet said to them, “Indeed, Allah has sent you Talut[1]as a king.” They said, “How can he have authority over us when we are more worthy of authority than he, for he was not brought abundance of wealth?” He said, “Allah has chosen him over you and has increased him in knowledge and build.” Thus Allah brings His authority to whomever He wills, for Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing.

footnotes.text: Saul.

2:248.annotated: And their prophet said to them, “Indeed, the sign of his authority is that the ark[1]shall come to you with tranquility from your Lord, and relics left by Moses’s folk and Aaron’s folk.(It shall be) carried by the angels. In that is a sign for you, if you have been believers.”

footnotes.text: Of the covenant.

2:249.annotated: So when Talut<sup>a </sup>set out with the troops, he said, “Allah will indeed be testing you with a river. So whoever drinks from it does not belong with me, but whoever does not taste it does belong with me—except for whoever scoops up a scoopful[1] with his hand.” Yet they drank from it, except for a few of them. Then when he had crossed it together with those who had attained faith with him, they said, “We have no strength to face Galut[2]and his troops today.” Those expecting to meet Allah said, “How many a small battalion has overcome a large battalion by Allah’s leave, for Allah is with the patient ones.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . scoops up a (single) scoop with his hand.”
Goliath.

2:251.annotated: So they defeated them by Allah’s leave when David killed Galut<sup>d </sup>, and Allah brought him authority and wisdom and taught him as He willed. And were it not for Allah repelling[1] some people by means of others, the earth would indeed become corrupted, but Allah is Gracious to all realms.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “And were it not for Allah strongly repelling some people . . .”

2:252.annotated: Those are Allah’s signs[1]which We read to you in truth, for you are most surely one of the emissaries.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

2:253.annotated: Those messengers—we favored some of them over others of them: to some of them Allah spoke(directly) , and some of them He elevated by degrees. And We[1]brought Jesus, son of Mary, the evident proofs, and We aided him with the Holy Spirit. And had Allah willed, those who succeeded them would not have fought one another after the evident proofs had come to them, but they disputed—for some of them attained faith and some of them denied. For had Allah willed, they would not have fought one another, but Allah does what He wants.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

2:255.annotated: Allah—there is no god but He, the Living, the All-Sustaining. Neither slumber overtakes Him nor sleep. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth. Who is it who can intercede with Him except by His leave? He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass any of His knowledge except according to what He wills. His knowledge[1]has embraced the heavens and the earth, and their preservation does not fatigue Him, for He is the All-High, the Great.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘His seat’.

2:258.annotated: Have you<sup>sg </sup>not seen the one who debated Abraham[1] about his Lord—that Allah had given him authority? Recall when Abraham<sup>c </sup>said, “My Lord is the One Who gives life and causes death.” He said, “I give life and cause death.” Abraham<sup>c </sup>said, “But surely, Allah brings the sun from the East, so you bring it from the West.” Thus the denier was confounded, for Allah does not guide the unjust<sup>pl </sup>.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham and Ibn Zekwan in one of his narrations read it as: “Abraham ”.

2:259.annotated: Or like the one who passed by a town and it was completely devastated upon its trellises. He said, “How can Allah revive this after its death?” Thereupon Allah caused him to die for a hundred years and then resurrected him. He said, “For how long have you tarried?” He said, “I have tarried for a day or part of a day.” He said, “Rather, you have tarried for a hundred years. And look at your food and your drink—it has not spoiled—and look at your donkey. And We will make you a sign for mankind. And look at the bones—how We assemble[1] them, then clothe them with flesh.” So when it became evident to him, he said, “I know[2] that Allah is All-Powerful over everything.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . how We revivify them,”
Qira’at: Hamza and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “So when it became evident to him, He said, “Know that . . .”

2:260.annotated: And recall when Abraham[1] said, “My Lord, show me how You revive the dead<sup>pl </sup>.” He said, “Have you not attained faith?” He said, “Yes indeed, but that my heart may become serene.” He said, “So take four birds and bend them towards you[2], then place on every mountain a part of them, then call them and they will come to you, running. And know that Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham and Ibn Zekwan in one of his narrations read it as: “Abraham ”.
According to Ibn ʻAbbas and other exegetes, ‘bend them’ is a metaphor for ‘cut them’.

2:262.annotated: Those who spend their wealths in the way of Allah and then do not follow up what they have spent with any reminder[1]or any harm—their reward is with their Lord, and no fear[2] shall beupon them nor shall they grieve.

footnotes.text: Of their generosity.
Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and no fear shall ever be upon them nor shall they grieve.”

2:264.annotated: O you who have attained faith, do not nullify your donations with reminders and hurtfulness, like one who spends his wealth for show in front of people and does not believe in Allah and the Last Day. His likeness is that of a smooth rock with dust upon it, then a heavy rain struck it and left it bare. They[1]have no power to retain anything of what they have earned. For Allah does not guide the denying people.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:269.annotated: He brings wisdom to whomever He wills, and whoever is brought[1] wisdom, then he has most surely beenbrought much good. But none constantly remembers except those of understanding.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and whoever He brings wisdom , then he has most surely been brought much good.

2:271.annotated: If you<sup>pl </sup>disclose donations, then that is excellent. But if you<sup>pl </sup>hide them and bring them to the needy, then that is better for you. And He will remit[1] your evil deeds for you. For Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i, Abu Jaʻfar and Khalaf read it as: “. . . then that is better for you, and We will (also) remit your evil deeds for you.”Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Shuʻba and Yaʻqub read it as: “then that is better for you. And We will remit your evil deeds for you.”

2:274.annotated: Those who spend their wealths by night and day, secretly and publicly—their reward is with their Lord, and no fear[1] shall beupon them nor shall they grieve.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and no fear shall ever be upon them nor shall they grieve.”

2:275.annotated: Those who devour usury cannot stand[1]except as does one who is being beaten by Satan into insanity. That is because they said, “Trade and usury are certainly the same.” But Allah has permitted trade and has forbidden usury. Thus, to whomsoever an admonition came from his Lord, so he refrained(from usury) —then his past earnings belong to him and his matter rests with Allah. Yet whoever reverts—then those[2]are the fellows of the Fire; therein they abide.

footnotes.text: On the Day of Resurrection.
A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

2:277.annotated: Indeed, those who have attained faith and have done righteous deeds and have established the prayer and have brought[1]the purifying charity[2]—their reward is with their Lord, and no fear<sup>a </sup>shall beupon them nor shall they grieve.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

2:279.annotated: But if you<sup>pl </sup>do not, then be informed[1] of a war from Allah and His Messenger. Yet if you repent, then your capitals belong to you—(thus) you do no injustice, and you are not done injustice.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba and Hamza read it as: “. . . then inform (everyone) of a war . . .”

2:280.annotated: But if he[1]has hardship, then deferment until a time of ease. But to donate[2]it is better for you<sup>pl </sup>, if you only knew.

footnotes.text: The debtor.
To waive it as charity.

2:281.annotated: And be mindful of a day[1]when you<sup>pl </sup>are returned[2] to Allah, then the earnings of every single self are rendered in full to it, for they[3]are not done injustice.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘guard yourselves against a day’.
Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . when you return to Allah . . .”
A grammatical shift from 2<sup>nd </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

2:282.annotated: O you who have attained faith, when you transact a debt for a stated term, write it down. And have a scribe write between you, in fairness. And let no scribe refuse to write as Allah has taught him. So let him write, and let the one upon whom is the duty of payment<sup>g </sup>dictate. And let him be mindful of Allah, his Lord, and defraud nothing of it. But if the one upon whom is the duty of payment is mentally deficient or weak or unable to dictate, then let his guardian dictate with fairness. And call to witness two of your men, but if the two are not men, then one man and two women from those whom you<sup>pl </sup>approve of as witnesses—so that if one of them should err[1] , the other can remind her. And witnesses must not abstain when called upon. And be not averse to writing it down, whether small or large(in value) , including its term. That is more just with Allah[2]and more upright for testimony and more likely to make you not doubt—except in the case of an immediate bargain you conduct among yourselves—for(then) you commit no sin if you do not write it down. But(otherwise) let there be witnesses whenever you trade with one another. And let no harm befall any scribe or witness, for if you ever do so, it shall be ungodliness on your part. And be mindful of Allah, and Allah teaches you, for Allah is All-Knowing of everything.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “…so that in case one of them errs, the other reminds her .”
That is more just than oral agreements.

2:285.annotated: The Messenger has attained faith in what was sent down to him from his Lord, as have the believers. They have all attained faith in Allah and His angels and His scriptures[1] and His messengers: “We make[2] no distinction between any of His messengers.” And they said, “We have heard and obeyed.(Grant us) Your forgiveness, our Lord, for to You is the destiny.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “scripture ”.
Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “He makes no distinction . . .”

3:7.annotated: It is He Who sent down upon you<sup>sg </sup>the Scripture. Some of its signs are explicit; they are the foundation[1]of the Scripture, while others are equivocal. So as for those whose hearts swerve, they follow whatever is equivocal of it, seeking tribulation and seeking its interpretation. But none knows its interpretation except Allah. Thus, those firmly rooted in knowledge say, “We have attained faith in it; all is from our Lord.” But none constantly remembers except those with understanding.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘the mother of the Scripture’.

3:9.annotated: “Our Lord, You will certainly gather mankind for a day about which there is no doubt.” Indeed, Allah[1]never breaks a promise.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 2<sup>nd </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

3:11.annotated: Like the behavior of Pharaoh’s folk and those before them: they disbelieved in Our signs, so Allah[1]seized them on account of their misdeeds. For Allah is Stern in retribution.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

3:12.annotated: Say<sup>sg </sup>to those who have denied, “You[1] shall be overcome and herded to Hell, so what a miserable resting place!”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “Say<sup>sg </sup>to those who have denied that they shall be overcome and herded to Hell, so what a miserable resting place!”

3:13.annotated: Surely, there was a sign for you<sup>pl </sup>in two battalions that met: one battalion combating in the way of Allah and another denying, seeing[1] them[2] —as the eyesees—twice their number. For Allah aids with His support whomever He wills. In that is indeed a lesson for those endowed with sight(s) .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Yaʻqub and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . and another denying. You <sup>pl </sup> see them—as the eye sees—twice their number.”
A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

3:19.annotated: Indeed[1] , religion with Allah is Islam. Yet those who were brought the Scripture did not differ with each other except after knowledge had come to them, thereby oppressing one another. So whoever denies the signs of Allah—then Allah is indeed Swift in reckoning.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Al Kesa’i read it as: “(And) that religion with Allah is Islam.”

3:20.annotated: So if they debate with you<sup>sg </sup>, then say, “I have submitted my countenance to Allah, and(so have) those who have followed me.” And say to those who were brought the Scripture and to the gentiles[1], “Have you submitted?” Thus, if they have submitted, then they have been guided. But if they turn away, then your(only) duty is proclamation, for Allah is All-Seeing of the servants.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘the unlettered’.

3:21.annotated: Indeed, those who deny Allah’s signs[1]and unjustifiably kill the prophets and kill[2] those of mankind who command to justice—give them glad tidings[3]of a painful punishment.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.
Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “. . . and combat those of mankind . . .”
This is said in sarcasm.

3:23.annotated: Have you<sup>sg </sup>not seen those who were brought a share of the Scripture, being called to the Scripture of Allah to judge[1] between them, then a group of them turn away in disregard?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . being called to the Scripture of Allah so that it may be judged between them . . .”

3:25.annotated: So how about when We gather them for a day about which there is no doubt, and every single self is paid in full for what it has earned, and they[1]are not dealt with unjustly?

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

3:36.annotated: So when she gave birth to her, she said, “My Lord, I have indeed given birth to her, a female,” and Allah knows better what she has delivered[1] , “and the maleis not like the female, and I have indeed named her Mary, and I do seek refuge with You for her and her offspring from Satan, the outcast.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, Shuʻba and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . a female, and Allah knows better what I have delivered, and the male is not . . .”

3:37.annotated: So her Lord accepted her with good acceptance and brought her up a good upbringing and entrusted her to the sponsorship of Zechariah[1] . Whenever Zechariah entered upon her in the sanctuary, he found with her provision[2]. He said, “O Mary, how did you get this?” She said, “It is from Allah; indeed, Allah provides whomever He wills without measure.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and Zechariah sponsored her .”
Food.

3:39.annotated: So the angels called[1] out to him as he stood praying in the sanctuarythat: “Allah gives[2] you glad tidings of John, confirming a Word from Allah, and honorable, and abstinent from women, and a prophet from among the righteous.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “So (one of) the angels called out to him . . .”
Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer and Hamza read it as: “. . . sanctuary: “Indeed , Allah gives you . . .”

3:47.annotated: She said, “My Lord, how can I have a child when no human being has touched me?” He said, “So shall it be! Allah creates whatever He wills. Whenever He decrees a matter, He only says to it, ‘Be,’ and so it is[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “He only says to it, ‘Be,’ so it is.”

3:48.annotated: And He[1] will teach himscribing[2]and wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ, ʻAsem, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “And We will teach him . . .”
The Arabic word used is al-kitabwhich may mean ‘scribing’ or ‘scripture’.

3:49.annotated: And(He will appoint him as) a messenger to the Children of Israel(to proclaim) : ‘I have come to you<sup>pl </sup>with a sign from your Lord: that I[1] createfor you out of clay the shape of a bird, then I breathe into it so it becomes a bird by Allah’s leave; and I heal the born-blind and the leper; and I revive the dead by Allah’s leave; and I inform you concerning what you eat and what you store in your houses. Indeed, in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . from your Lord: I truly create . . .”

3:52.annotated: So when Jesus sensed denial on their part, he said, “Who are my supporters towards Allah?” The disciples said, “We are Allah’s supporters; we have attained faith in Allah, so bear witness that we are indeed Muslims[1].

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Muslimoonwhich means those who willingly submit to God, regardless of which prophet they followed.

3:54.annotated: And they[1]schemed and Allah schemed, but Allah is the best of schemers.

footnotes.text: The disbelievers.

3:57.annotated: And as for those who have attained faith and have done righteous deeds—He[1] will render[2] to themtheir rewards in full, for Allah does not love the unjust.”

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
Qira’at: All except for Hafs and Roways read it as: “We will render to them . . .” (In this case there is no grammatical shift).

3:58.annotated: This is what We read to you<sup>sg </sup>of the signs[1]and the Wise Reminder.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

3:64.annotated: Say, “O People of the Scripture, come to a common word between us and you: that we worship none but Allah, and that we associate nothing with Him, and that we do not take one another as lords apart from Allah.” And if they turn away, then say<sup>pl </sup>, “Bear witness that we are Muslims[1].”

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Muslimoonwhich means those who willingly submit to God, regardless of which prophet they followed.

3:73.annotated: But trust none except whoever has followed your<sup>pl </sup>religion.” Say<sup>sg </sup>“Indeed,(true) guidance is(only) Allah’s guidance—that[1] anyone can be brought the like of what you<sup>pl </sup>were brought, or they[2] maydebate with you before your Lord.” Say, “All grace is in Allah’s hand; He gives it to whomever He wills.” For Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “. . . Allah’s guidance. Can anyone be brought the like of what you<sup>pl </sup>were brought, or can they debate with you before your Lord?”
A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

3:75.annotated: And of the People of the Scripture is one who, if you<sup>sg </sup>entrust him with a heap(of gold) , will pay it back to you. And of them is one who, if you entrust him with a(single) dinar, will not pay it back to you unless you are constantly standing over him. That is because they have said, “We are under no obligation towards the gentiles[1].” And they tell lies against Allah, though they know.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘the unlettered’.

3:76.annotated: Yes[1], whoever fulfills his covenant and is mindful(of God) —then indeed, Allah loves mindful people.

footnotes.text: Answering their claim that they are under no obligation towards the gentiles.

3:79.annotated: No person to whom Allah has given the Scripture and wise judgment and prophethood would ever say to mankind, “Be my servants apart from Allah.” Rather, “Be godly[1]on account of the Scripture which you<sup>pl </sup>used to teach[2] and on account of what you used to learn.”

footnotes.text: Literally ‘Lordly’.
Qira’at: All except for Ibn ʻAmer, ʻAsem, Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . used to know and . . .”

3:80.annotated: Nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords. Would he command you to denial after you became Muslims[1]?

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Muslimoonwhich means those who willingly submit to God, regardless of which prophet they followed.

3:81.annotated: And recall when Allah took the pledge of the(followers of the) prophets, “Inasmuch as I[1] have given you<sup>pl </sup>of scripture and wisdom, should a messengercometo you confirming what you have, you shall certainly believe in him and you shall certainly support him.” He said, “Have you consented and taken up that heavy load towards Me upon yourselves?” They said, “We have consented.” He said, “Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “Inasmuch as We have given you . . .”Hamza read it as: “Because of what I have given you of scripture and wisdom, then a messenger has come to you . . .”

3:83.annotated: Do they[1] seekother than the religion of Allah, when to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly and reluctantly, and to Him they will be returned[2] ?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Abu ʻAmr, Hafs and Yaʻqub read it as: “Do you <sup>pl </sup>seek . . .”
Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “and to Him they return .” All except for Hafs and Yaʻqub read it as: “and to Him you <sup>pl </sup>return .”

3:84.annotated: Say<sup>sg </sup>, “We have attained faith in Allah, and in what was sent down upon us, and in what was sent down upon Abraham and Ishmael and Isaac and Jacob and the Grandsons[1], and in what was brought to Moses and Jesus and the prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them, and to Him we are Muslims<sup>b </sup>.”

footnotes.text: The different prophets of the Israelites.

3:93.annotated: All food was permissible to the Children of Israel except what Israel forbade for himself before the Torah was bestowed from on high[1] . Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Bring the Torah and read it, if you<sup>pl </sup>are truthful.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . before the Torah was sent down .”

3:101.annotated: And how could you deny when Allah’s signs[1]are being read to you and among you is His Messenger? And whoever holds fast to Allah has surely been guided to a straight path.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

3:106.annotated: on a day when some faces are whitened and some faces are blackened. So as for those whose faces were[1]blackened: “Did you deny after having attained faith?” Then taste the punishment on account of what you used to deny.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

3:109.annotated: Thus, to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, Hamza, Al Kesa’i, Yaʻqub and Khalaf read it as: “. . . and to Allah all matters return .”

3:113.annotated: They are not alike: of the People of the Scripture is a community that is upright—they read Allah’s signs[1]throughout the night while prostrating themselves.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

3:115.annotated: And whatever good they[1] do, they will not be denied it, for Allah is All-Knowing of those who are mindful(of Him) .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except Hafs, Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “And whatever good you <sup>pl </sup>do, you will not be denied it . . .”

3:123.annotated: And Allah had very truly given you<sup>pl </sup>support at Badr when you were humble[1]. So be mindful of Allah, that you may give thanks.

footnotes.text: They were lesser in number and in weaponry.

3:124.annotated: Recall saying<sup>sg </sup>to the believers, “Shall it not suffice you that your Lord should help you with three thousand angels sent down[1] ?”

footnotes.text: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . three thousand angels bestowed from on high ?”

3:125.annotated: Yes indeed,(but) if you<sup>pl </sup>persevere patiently and become mindful(of God) and they attack you suddenly, your Lord will aid you with five thousand angelshaving marks[1] (of distinction).

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, ʻAsem and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . five thousand marked angels .”

3:133.annotated: And[1] hastentowards forgiveness from your<sup>pl </sup>Lord and a Garden as wide as the heavens and the earth, prepared for the mindful(of God) :

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “Hasten towards . . .”

3:140.annotated: If a blow touches you, a similar blow has surely touched the(other) people. For such days We alternate between mankind, and so that Allah[1]may know those who have attained faith and take witnesses[2]from among you. For Allah does not love the unjust.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
The Arabic word used is shuhada’, which literally means ‘witnesses’ and is usually used to describe martyrs.

3:145.annotated: For never was it for anyone to die except by Allah’s leave at a predetermined time. So whoever wants the recompense of the Earlier(Life) , We[1]bring him of it. And whoever wants the recompense of the Hereafter, We bring him of it. And We will repay the thankful ones.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

3:146.annotated: And how many a prophet has had numerous godly[1]people combating[2] alongside him? And they did not waver regardless of that which afflicted them in the way of Allah, nor did they weaken, nor did they give in. And Allah loves the patient ones.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘Lordly’.
Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . numerous godly people killed alongside him?”

3:151.annotated: We will throw terror into the hearts of those who have denied because they associated with Allah[1](partners) for which He bestowedfrom on high[2] no authority. And their shelter is the Fire, and how miserable is the dwelling of the unjust!

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . for which He sent down no authority.”

3:153.annotated: Recall climbing<sup>pl </sup>and not looking back for anyone, with the Messenger calling you from your rear[1]. Then He repaid you with sorrow on account of the sorrow(you caused the prophet) so that you would not grieve over what you missed or for what befell you. For Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

footnotes.text: At the battle of Uhud, the Muslims fled the battlefield upon their defeat and the Prophet (peace be upon him) stood calling them to come back and fight.

3:154.annotated: Then after the stress He sent down upon you<sup>pl </sup>security(in the form of)drowsiness overcoming[1] a faction of you, while a faction cared only for themselves, assuming about Allah contrary to the truth—assumptions of the era of ignorance[2]—saying, “Is anything up to us?” Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Everything is up to Allah.” They hide within themselves what they do not disclose to you. They say, “If it were up to us, none of us would have been killed here.” Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Even if you had stayed in your houses, those destined to be killed would have emerged to their death beds.” And so that Allah may test what is in your chests and so that He may purge what is in your hearts, for Allah is All-Knowing of what lies within the chests.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “He sent down upon you<sup>pl </sup>security overcoming a faction of you (in the form of) a nap , while a faction . . .”
The Arabic word used is jahiliyahwhich is derived from jahl, meaning ‘ignorance’, and refers to the pre-Islamic phase of paganism.

3:156.annotated: O you who have attained faith, do not be like those who denied and said of their brethren who traveled in the land or were on an expedition, “Had they stayed with us, they would not have died or got killed.” So that Allah may make it a cause of regret in their hearts. For Allah gives life and causes death, and Allah is All-Seeing of what you<sup>pl </sup>do[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . and Allah is All-Seeing of what they do .”

3:157.annotated: Thus if you<sup>pl </sup>get killed in the way of Allah or die—surely, forgiveness and mercy from Allah are better than what they[1] hoard.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs read it as: “. . . better than what you <sup>pl </sup>hoard .”

3:161.annotated: And never was it for a prophet to defraud[1] , for whoever defrauds brings whatever he has defrauded on the Day of Resurrection. Then every single self is paid in full for what it has earned, and they are not dealt with unjustly.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and ʻAsem read it as: “And never was it for a prophet to be defrauded . . .”

3:168.annotated: Those who said of their brethren, as they stayed behind, “Had they obeyed us, they would not have been killed[1] .” Say, “Then avert death from yourselves, if you are truthful.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hisham read it as: “. . . they would not have been relentlessly killed .”

3:169.annotated: And never[1] think<sup>sg </sup>of those killed[2] in the way of Allah as dead. Rather,(they are) alive, with their Lord, being provided for,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hisham—in one of his recitations—read it as: “And never should he think of those killed in the . . .”
Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “And never think<sup>sg </sup>of those relentlessly killed in the way of Allah as dead.”

3:170.annotated: exulting over what Allah has brought them out of His grace and glad for those behind them who have not yet joined them: that no fear[1] shall beupon them nor shall they grieve.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . that no fear shall ever be upon them nor shall they grieve.”

3:178.annotated: And never should those who have denied think[1] that We respite them for their own good. In fact, We only respite them so that they may increase in sin, for for them is a demeaning punishment.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “And never think <sup>sg </sup>—regarding those who have denied— that We respite them . . .”

3:180.annotated: And never should those who are miserly with what Allah has given them of His grace think[1] that it is good for them. Rather, it is an evil thing for them. They will be encircled by whatever they were miserly with on the Day of Resurrection, for to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth. And Allah is All-Aware of whatever you<sup>pl </sup>do[2] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “And never think <sup>sg </sup>—regarding those who are miserly with what Allah has given them of His grace— that it is good for them.”
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . of whatever they do .”

3:181.annotated: Allah has most surely heard the statement of those who said, “Indeed, Allah is poor while we are rich.” We[1] will[2] writedown what they said and their unjustified killing of the prophets, and Wewill say, “Taste the punishment of the burning.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.
Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “He will write down what they said and their unjustified killing of the prophets, and He will say . . .” (In this case there is no grammatical shift.)

3:184.annotated: So if they disbelieve you<sup>sg </sup>, messengers before you were disbelieved. They came with clear proofs and Books andthe illuminating Scripture[1].

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hisham read it as: “. . . and with Books and with the illuminating Scripture.”Ibn Zekwan read it as: “. . . and with Books and the illuminating Scripture.”

3:187.annotated: And as Allah took a pledge from those who were brought the Scripture: “Most surely you[1] shall make it evidentto mankind and not conceal it.” But they tossed it behind their backs and purchased, in exchange for it, a small price, so how miserable is what they purchase!

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Shuʻba read it as: “Most surely they shall make it evident . . .”

3:188.annotated: Never[1] think<sup>sg </sup>ofthose who exult over what they have come up with and love to be praised for what they have not done—never think<sup>sg </sup>of them as in a place safe from the punishment, for for them is a painful punishment.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “Never should they think—those who exult over what they have come up with and love to be praised for what they have not done, never should they think of them(selves) as in a place safe from the punishment . . .”Nafieʻ read it as: “Never should they think—those who exult over what they have come up with and love to be praised for what they have not done, never think <sup>sg </sup>of them as in a place safe from the punishment . . .”

3:195.annotated: So their Lord responded to them: “I do not waste the work of any worker of you, whether male or female—you are of one another. So those who emigrated and were evicted from their homes and were hurt in my way and(who) combated and were killed[1] —I will most surely remit for them their evil deeds and will most surely admit them into Gardens beneath which rivers flow—a recompense from Allah, for with Allah is the excellent recompense.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . and were killed and (who) combated . . .” Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . and (who) combated and were relentlessly killed . . .”

3:199.annotated: And indeed, of the People of the Scripture are those who believe in Allah and in what was sent down to you and in what was sent down to them. They are reverent towards Allah and do not purchase, in exchange for Allah’s signs[1], a small price. Those have their reward with their Lord. Indeed, Allah is Swift in reckoning.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

4:1.annotated: O mankind, be mindful of your Lord, Who created you from a single self and created from it its spouse, and from them both spread many men and women. Thus be mindful of Allah—in Whose name you ask one another—and of the[1] wombs[2] . Indeed, Allah has always been Watchful over you.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “Thus be mindful of Allah,in Whose name, and the name of the wombs, you ask one another .”
The term ‘wombs’ is usually used in the Qur’an as a metaphor for blood relatives, meaning: honor the ties of kinship.

4:3.annotated: And if you<sup>pl </sup>fear you cannot be just towards the orphans, then marry the women you like—two or three or four—but if you fear you will not be equitable, then(only) one[1] or(consider) those whom you rightfully possess. That is more likely to make you avoid bias.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . then (only) one (is enough) or consider . . .”

4:6.annotated: And test the orphans until they reach the age of marriage. So if you<sup>pl </sup>recognize in them prudence, then hand over their wealths to them and do not devour it extravagantly or hastily before they grow up. For the rich(guardian) should modestly abstain(from charging any wage) , but whoever(of the guardians) is poor may charge[1]in accordance with what is fair. Then when you hand over their wealths to them, call witnesses in. Yet sufficient is Allah as a Reckoner.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘devour’.

4:10.annotated: Indeed, those who devour the wealths of orphans illicitly devour only fire into their bellies; and they will roast[1] in a blaze.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer and Shuʻba read it as: “. . . and they will be roasted in the blaze.”

4:11.annotated: Allah enjoins you<sup>pl </sup>regarding your children: for the male is the equivalent of the share of two females. But if they are women above two, they get two-thirds of what he has left; and if she be one, then to her is the half. And for his parents—each gets one-sixth of what he has left if he has children. Yet if he has no children and his parents inherit(solely) from him, then his mother getsone-third. But if he has siblings, then his mother gets one-sixth, after(fulfilling) any bequest he may bequeath[1] and(paying off) any debt. Your parents[2]and your children—you do not know which are more beneficial to you.(This is) an ordinance from Allah. Indeed, Allah has always been All-Knowing All-Wise.
