16:27.annotated: Then, on the Day of Resurrection, He disgraces them and says, “Where are My associates for whose sake you used to oppose[1] (the believers) ? Those who were given knowledge said[2], “Today disgrace and misery are indeed upon the deniers

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ read it as: “. . . for whose sake you used to oppose Me ?”
Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

16:28.annotated: whom the angels take at death while they are unjust to themselves.” Then they offered submission[1]: “We were doing no evil.” Yes! Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of what you<sup>pl </sup>used to do.

footnotes.text: After death.

16:36.annotated: For very truly, in every community We sent a messenger: “Worship<sup>pl </sup>Allah and avoid false masters.” So some of them Allah has guided, and some of them have deserved misguidance. So journey[1]through the earth and look what the outcome was for the disbelievers.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 2<sup>nd </sup>person.

16:37.annotated: (Even) if you<sup>sg </sup>are concerned about their guidance,(still) Allah surely does not guide whomever He leads[1] astray, and they will have no helpers.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . (still) whomever Allah leads astray surely cannot be guided . . .”

16:40.annotated: Indeed, Our only saying to anything, once We have wanted it, is to say to it, “Be,” and so it is[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “. . . is to say to it, ‘Be,’ so it is.”

16:42.annotated: Those are the ones who endured patiently, and in their Lord they place[1]their trust.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from past tense to present tense.

16:43.annotated: And never did We send as messengers before you<sup>sg </sup>except men to whom We reveal[1] . So ask<sup>pl </sup>the people of the Reminder if you do not know.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs read it as: “. . . to whom it is revealed .”

16:48.annotated: Have they[1] not seenall things that Allah has created—their shadows revolving from the right and the left, prostrating to Allah as they shrink away?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “Have you <sup>pl </sup>not seen . . .”

16:51.annotated: And Allah has said: “Do<sup>pl </sup>not take two gods; He is but One God, so of Me[1]alone be in awe.”

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

16:56.annotated: And they set up to what they do not know a share of what We have provided for them. By Allah, you[1]will surely be asked about what you<sup>pl </sup>used to fabricate.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 2<sup>nd </sup>person.

16:58.annotated: But when one of them is given the glad tidings[1]of a female(infant) , his countenance remains darkened as he suppresses his anguish.

footnotes.text: Said in sarcasm.

16:61.annotated: And if Allah were to hold mankind for their injustices, He would not leave upon it a single treading creature, but He defers them to a stated term. Then, when their term has arrived[1], they cannot delay it by one hour nor can they advance it.

footnotes.text: By death.

16:62.annotated: And they set up for Allah what they themselves hate, while their tongues describe the lie that theirs is the best(reward) ; without doubt, for them is the Fire and(without doubt) they will be driven to it quickly[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . for them is the Fire and (without doubt) they have been neglecting (their tasks) ”.Nafie read it as: “. . . for them is the Fire and (without doubt) they have gone too far .”

16:66.annotated: And indeed, there is a lesson for you<sup>pl </sup>in livestock: We[1] give you to drinkof what is in their bellies—from between filth and blood—pure milk, palatable to the drinkers.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . livestock: they give you to drink . . .”

16:71.annotated: And Allah has favored some of you over others in provision, yet those who were favored do not give their provision to those whom they rightfully possess, to the extent of making them equal partners in it. Do they[1] then repudiatethe blessing of Allah?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba and Roways read it as: “Do you <sup>pl </sup>then repudiate . . .”

16:72.annotated: And Allah has set up for you spouses from among yourselves, and has assigned for you from your spouses, children and grandchildren, and has provided you with good things. Yet is it in falsehood that they[1]believe, while it is the blessing of Allah that they deny?

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 2<sup>nd </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

16:75.annotated: Allah set forth a parable: an owned bondman who has no power over anything, and(on the other hand) someone to whom We[1]have given goodly provision from which he gives, secretly and openly. Can they be equal? All praise be to Allah; rather, most of them know not.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

16:79.annotated: Have they[1] not seenthe birds subjected in the midst of the sky? None holds them up except Allah. Surely, in that are signs for people who believe.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, Hamza, Yaʻqub and Khalaf read it as: “Have you <sup>pl </sup>not seen . . .”

16:82.annotated: So if they[1]turn away, then certainly your<sup>sg </sup>only duty is evident proclamation.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 2<sup>nd </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

16:86.annotated: And when the ones who associated(others with God) see their associates[1], they will say, “Our Lord, these are our associates whom we used to call upon apart from You.” So they cast[2]to them the statement, “Very truly, you are liars.”

footnotes.text: The false gods.
Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

16:88.annotated: Those who denied and barred from the way of Allah—We[1]added punishment to their punishment on account of the corruption they used to cause.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

16:89.annotated: And on a day when We raise in every community a witness against them from among them, and We brought<sup>c </sup>you<sup>sg </sup>as a witness against these. For We have bestowed upon you the Scripture from on high, as an explanation of everything and guidance and mercy and glad tidings for the Muslims[1].

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Muslimeenwhich means those who willingly submit to God, regardless of which prophet they followed.

16:90.annotated: Indeed, Allah commands to justice and excelling in doing good and bringing[1](charity) to the relative, and He forbids obscenity and what is deplorable and oppression. He admonishes you, that you may remind yourselves[2] .

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . that you may constantly remember .”

16:96.annotated: What you have runs out, but what is with Allah remains. And We[1] will most surely repaythose who were patient their reward in accordance with the best of what they used to do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Ibn Kathir, ʻAsem, Abu Jaʻfar and Ibn Zekwan in one of his narrations read it as: “And He will most surely repay . . .”

16:97.annotated: Whoever has acted righteously, whether male or female, while being a believer—We will most surely grant him a good life, and We will most surely repay them[1]their reward in accordance with the best of what they used to do.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

16:98.annotated: So when you<sup>sg </sup>recite the Recital[1]seek refuge with Allah from Satan, the outcast.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’an which literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

16:101.annotated: Yet whenever We substitute a sign in place of another sign—and Allah[1]knows better what He bestows from on high[2] —they say, “Indeed, you are nothing but a fabricator.” Rather, most of them do not know.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . what He sends down . . .”

16:102.annotated: Say, The Holy Spirit has bestowed it from on high from your<sup>sg </sup>Lord[1], with the truth, in order to strengthen those who have attained faith, and as guidance and glad tidings for Muslims[2].

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 2<sup>nd </sup>person.
The Arabic word used is Muslimeenwhich means those who willingly submit to God, regardless of which prophet they followed.

16:106.annotated: Whoever has denied Allah after attaining faith—except for someone who was compelled[1]while his heart rests securely in faith, but(rather) whoever(willingly) opens a chest to denial—upon them is wrath from Allah, and for them is a great punishment.

footnotes.text: God excuses anyone who is compelled to renounce his/her faith.

16:122.annotated: And We[1]brought him goodness in the Earlier(Life) , and in the Hereafter he is surely of the righteous.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

17:1.annotated: Highly Exalted is the One Who took His servant on a journey by night from the Inviolable Mosque[1]to the Farthest Mosque[2], whose precincts We<sup>a </sup>have blessed, in order to show him of Our signs; indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.

footnotes.text: Al-masjid Al-Harāmin Makkah.
Al-masjid Al-Aqsain Jerusalem.

17:2.annotated: And We brought Moses the Scripture and made it guidance for the Children of Israel: “Take[1] none for trustee other than Me,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . for the Children of Israel, that they may take none for trustee other than Me.

17:7.annotated: If you excel in doing good, you excel in doing good to your own benefit; and if you do evil, you do so against yourselves. Then when the promise of the second time comes true, they[1] will defileyour faces, and they will enter the Mosque as they entered it the first time, and they will utterly destroy all that falls into their power.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, Shuʻba, Hamza and Khalaf read it as: “. . . He will defile . . .” Al-Kesa’i read it as: “. . . We will defile . . .”

17:8.annotated: Hopefully your<sup>pl </sup>Lord will have mercy on you. But if you revert, We[1]will revert. And We have made Hell a prison for the deniers.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

17:9.annotated: Indeed, this Recital[1]guides to what is most upright and gives glad tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that for them there is a supreme reward,

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’an which literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

17:12.annotated: And We have made the night and the day as two signs, then We erased the sign of the night and made the sign of the day as an eye-opener, that you<sup>pl </sup>may seek grace from your Lord[1]and that you may learn the number of years and the calculation; and everything have We explained in detail.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

17:13.annotated: And for every person We have attached his augury to his neck, and on the Day of Resurrection We will bring out for him a record[1] which he will find spread open[2] .

footnotes.text: Literally, ‘scripture’.

Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . and on the Day of Resurrection a record, which he will receive spread open, is brought out for him .”Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and on the Day of Resurrection a record, which he will find spread open, comes out for him .”Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . and on the Day of Resurrection We will bring out for him a record which he will receive spread open.”

17:16.annotated: And when We want to annihilate a town We command[1] its affluent ones(to be righteous) , yet they defiantly disobey(Our commands) in it, so it deserves the decree and We annihilate it completely.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . We make its affluent ones in command , yet they . . .”

17:17.annotated: And how many generations have We annihilated after Noah? Thus sufficient is your Lord[1]as All-Aware, All-Seeing of the misdeeds of His servants.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

17:18.annotated: Whoever has been wanting the hasty(life of this world) —We hasten for him therein whatever We will to whomever We desire. Then We assigned[1]for him Hell where he roasts, condemned, defeated.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

17:24.annotated: And lower to them the wing[1]of humility, out of mercy, and say, “My Lord, have mercy on both of them as they raised me when I was a child.”

footnotes.text: An expression that implies showing compassion.

17:28.annotated: But if you<sup>sg </sup>disregard them, seeking mercy[1]which you expect from your Lord, then speak to them using gentle words.

footnotes.text: According to exegetes, ‘mercy’ here means ‘provision’.

17:29.annotated: And do not keep your hand tied to your neck[1]nor spread it out fully, lest you end up blamed, regretful.

footnotes.text: A metaphor for miserliness.

17:33.annotated: And do<sup>pl </sup>not kill the self which Allah has made inviolable, except in the course of justice. And if someone is killed unjustly, We have given authority to his kinsman who seeks retribution, but he[1] should not be excessivein killing; indeed, he is bound to be aided.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . but you <sup>sg </sup>should not be excessive . . .”

17:38.annotated: All of that—its evil has always been[1] disliked by your Lord.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “All of thathas always been an evil deed before your <sup>sg </sup>Lord (and) disliked .”

17:40.annotated: Has your<sup>pl </sup>Lord favored you with sons and taken for Himself from the angels females? You<sup>pl </sup>are certainly saying a great[1]saying.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word azeemis sometimes used with a negative connotation to denote the seriousness of a matter.

17:41.annotated: And very truly, We have explained in this Recital[1]in various ways, that they may constantly remember[2] , but it only adds to their aversion.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’an which literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.
Qira’at: Hamza, Al Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . that they may remember . . .”

17:42.annotated: Say<sup>sg </sup>, “If there were other gods with Him as they[1] say, they would have sought a way to the Possessor of the Throne.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Ibn Kathir and Hafs read it as: “. . . as you <sup>pl </sup>say . . .”

17:45.annotated: And when you<sup>sg </sup>recite the Recital[1], We place between you and those who do not believe in the Hereafter an invisible barrier.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’an which literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

17:46.annotated: And We have placed veils over their hearts preventing them from comprehending it, and heaviness in their ears. And when you mention your Lord[1]alone in the Recital<sup>a </sup>, they turn their backs in aversion.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

17:49.annotated: And they said, “Can it be thatwhen we have become bones and fragments—can it be that[1] we will really be resurrected as a new creation?”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Al-Kesa’i and Yaʻqub read it as: “Can it be that when we have become bones and fragments we will really . . .” Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “When we have become bones and fragments—can it be that we will really . . .”

17:55.annotated: And your<sup>sg </sup>Lord knows better about whoever is in the heavens and the earth. And We[1]have most surely favored some prophets over others, and to David We gave a Book[2].

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.
The Zabooror the Psalms.

17:59.annotated: And nothing prevented Us from sending(miraculous) signs except that the ancients disbelieved in them. So We gave Thamûd[1]the she-camel as an eye-opener, but they mistreated it. For We never send signs except to frighten(people of destruction) .

footnotes.text: The pagan tribe of Prophet Salih.

17:60.annotated: And recall when We said to you<sup>sg </sup>that your Lord[1]has encompassed mankind. And We did not make the vision We showed you except as a means of trial for mankind, and(recall) the tree which is cursed in the Recital[2]. And We frighten them, but that increases them in nothing but supreme transgression.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

17:61.annotated: And recall when We said to the angels, “Prostrate to Adam,” so they prostrated—but not Iblis[1]. He said, “Shall I prostrate down to someone You created of clay?”

footnotes.text: Iblis is another name of Satan or Shaytan.

17:67.annotated: And when harm touches you<sup>pl </sup>at sea,(all) those you call upon become lost except for Him. But when He delivered[1]you to the shore, you disregarded(Him) ; thus man has always been a staunch denier.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from present tense to past tense.

17:68.annotated: Are you<sup>pl </sup>confident that He[1] will not cause a side of the shore to collapsebeneath you or unleash a tornado against you, and then you find no trustee?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . that We will not cause a side of the shore to collapse . . .”

17:69.annotated: Or are you<sup>pl </sup>confident that He[1] will not return youto it once again and unleash a hurricane of wind[2] against you anddrown[3] you for your denial, and then you find no attending followers against Us?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . that We will not return you to it once again and unleash . . .”
Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “winds ”.
Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar and Roways read it as: “. . . against you which then drowns you . . .”

17:71.annotated: On the day when We call every group of people by their leader, then whoever is given his record[1]in his right hand—those will read their record, and they will not be dealt with unjustly by as much as the hair upon a date-stone.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘scripture’.

17:78.annotated: Establish<sup>sg </sup>the prayer at the decline of the sun until the dusk of the night, as well as the Recitation[1]at dawn; indeed, Recitation at dawn has always been witnessed.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

17:82.annotated: And We bestow from on high[1] of the Recital<sup>d </sup>that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, but it does not increase the unjust except in loss.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “And We send down of the Recital that which . . .”

17:83.annotated: And when We bless man, he disregards(Us) and distances himself[1] . But when evil touches him, he staunchly despairs.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Zekwan and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . and turns his back (literally ‘his side’).”

17:87.annotated: except through a mercy from your Lord[1]; indeed, His grace upon you has been supreme.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

17:88.annotated: Say, “Most surely, if all humans and all unseen beings[1]were to come together to bring forth the like of this Recital[2], they could never bring forth the like of it, even if they backed up one another.”

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is jinnwhich are unseen beings that are accountable for their actions.
The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

17:93.annotated: or possess a house of gold; or ascend into the sky. Even then, we will not believe in your ascension until you bestowupon us from on high[1] a scripture that we can read.” Say, “Highly Exalted is my Lord. Have I been anything except a human messenger?”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . until you send down upon us a scripture that we can read.”

17:95.annotated: Say[1] , “If there were angels on earth walking around in peace, We would have bestowed upon them from heaven an angel messenger.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “He said . . .”

17:97.annotated: And whomever Allah guides is the guided one, and whomever He leads astray—for them[1]you will find no guardians apart from Him, and We will herd them on the Day of Resurrection on their faces, blind and dumb and deaf; their shelter is Hell; whenever it abates, We intensify the blaze for them.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

17:98.annotated: That is their repayment for having denied Our signs and for having said, “Can it be thatwhen we have become bones and fragments—can it be that[1] we will really be resurrected as a new creation?”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Al-Kesa’i and Yaʻqub read it as: “Can it be that when we have become bones and fragments we will really . . .” Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “When we have become bones and fragments—can it be that we will really . . .”

17:102.annotated: He said, “You<sup>sg </sup>have[1] most surely knownthat nonesent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth,(as) insights. And indeed I think that you, O Pharaoh, are doomed to demise.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Al Kesa’i read it as: “He said, ‘I have most surely known . . .’”

17:106.annotated: And a Recital[1]which We apportioned, that you<sup>sg </sup>may recite it to mankind leisurely. And We surely bestowed it from on high.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

18:9.annotated: Or did you<sup>sg </sup>think that the fellows of the cave and the Inscription[1]were among Our signs a wonder?

footnotes.text: A tablet recording their story.

18:17.annotated: And you<sup>sg </sup>see[1]the sun when it rises, veering away from their cave towards the right, and when it sets, moving away from them to the left as they lie in a hollow therein; that is of Allah’s signs. Whomever Allah guides is the(truly) guided one, but whomever He leads astray—for him you<sup>sg </sup>will find no guiding guardian.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from past tense to present tense, which serves to create a vivid portrait of past events.

18:21.annotated: And thus We caused them to be discovered, that they[1]would know that the promise of Allah[2]is true and that of the Hour there is no doubt. As they were disagreeing with each other about their affair, they said, “Build over them a structure.” Their Lord knows better about them. Those who prevailed over their affair[3]said, “We will set up over them a mosque[4].”

footnotes.text: The people of the city who discovered them.
A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
Literally ‘those who overcame (the others) in their affair’.
The Arabic word is masjidwhich literally means ‘a place for prostration’.

18:22.annotated: Some will say, “Three, their fourth being their dog.” And some will say, “Five, their sixth being their dog,” —guessing at the unknown. And some will say, “Seven, and their eighth being their dog.” Say<sup>sg </sup>, “My Lord knows better of their exact number”. None knows(the reality about) them except a few. So enter<sup>sg </sup>not into controversies concerning them except on a matter that is clear, and do not consult any of them[1]about them.

footnotes.text: The People of the Scripture.

18:26.annotated: Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Allah knows better how long they remained; to Him belongs the hidden realm of the heavens and the earth. How clearly He sees and how finely He hears! They have no guardian apart from Him, and He does[1] not associateanyone in His judgment.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . and do not associate anyone in His judgement.”

18:28.annotated: And keep<sup>sg </sup>yourself patient in the company of those who pray to their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Countenance[1], and do not turn your eyes away from them, seeking the adornment of the Earlier Life, and do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance[2]so that he has followed his own whim and his affairs have become confused.

footnotes.text: Al-Alousi and other exegetes interpreted this expression as ‘to please Him’.
The Arabic word zhikrcan be translated as ‘remembrance’, ‘reminder’ or ‘mentioning’.

18:30.annotated: Indeed, those who have attained faith and have done righteous deeds…[1]—indeed, We do not waste the reward of whoever excels in work.

footnotes.text: This sentence is left open-ended; according Az-Zamakhshari its predicate is sign 31.

18:31.annotated: For those, there are the Gardens of Eden,rivers flowing beneath them. In it, they are[1]adorned with bracelets of gold and wear green garments of silk and brocade, reclining therein on couches. What a wonderful recompense, and what an excellent place of rest!

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift to present tense, which serves to create a vivid portrait of future events.

18:34.annotated: And thus he had riches[1], so he said to his fellow as he conversed with him, “I am wealthier than you and greater in manpower.”

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is thamarwhich can be pronounced as thumror thumuraccording to the majority of reciters, and in all cases it also means ‘produce’.

18:36.annotated: and I do not think that the Hour is ever coming. And even if I am taken back to my Lord, I will most surely find something better than it[1] as a destination.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . better than them both as . . .”

18:44.annotated: In that situation, protection[1] belongs to Allah, the Truth; He is better in rewarding and better in requiting.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “In that situation, authority belongs to Allah . . .”

18:45.annotated: And set<sup>sg </sup>forth for them a parable for the Earlier Life:(it is) like water that We sent down from the sky, then the plants of the earth were mixed with it, so it became debris scattered by the wind[1] . And Allah[2]has always had absolute power over everything.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “winds ”
A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

18:47.annotated: And on the day when We set the mountains[1] in motionand you<sup>sg </sup>see the earth emerging; and We herded[2]them together and left none of them behind.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “And on the day when the mountains are set in motion . . .”
Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

18:49.annotated: And the record[1]was placed, and you<sup>sg </sup>see[2]the criminals fearful of whatever is in it, and they say, “Woe to us! What is with this record that leaves nothing, small or big, but it has enumerated it?” And they found[3]whatever they had done present(before them) , for your<sup>sg </sup>Lord is never unjust to anyone.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘scripture’.
A grammatical shift to present tense, which serves to create a vivid portrait of future events.
A grammatical shift, where the tense reverts to past tense.

18:50.annotated: And recall when We said to the angels, “Prostrate to Adam.” So they prostrated—but not Iblis[1]. He was one of the unseen beings[2], so he defied the command of his Lord. Will you take him and his offspring as guardians apart from Me when they are an enemy to you? What a miserable bargain for the unjust!

footnotes.text: Iblis is another name of Satan or Shaytan.
The Arabic word used is jinnwhich are unseen beings that are accountable for their actions.

18:51.annotated: I[1] did not make them witnessthe creation of the heavens and the earth, nor their own creation, and never was I to[2] takethe misguiding people for assistants.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “We did not make them witness . . .”
Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . and never were you to take the misguiding people for assistants.”

18:52.annotated: And on the day when He says[1] , “Call on My associates whom you have claimed.” So they called[2]on them, but they did not respond to them. And We[3]placed between them a barrier.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “. . . when We say . . .”
Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.
A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

18:54.annotated: And We have elaborated in this Recital[1]for mankind every kind of parable, but man has always been the most argumentative being.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’an which literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

18:55.annotated: And what prevented mankind from attaining faith when guidance came to them and from seeking their Lord’s forgiveness? Unless they are waiting for the rule of(God regarding) the ancients to come upon them or to have the punishment come upon themin many types[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . or to have the punishment come upon them face to face .”

18:56.annotated: And We do not send emissaries except as bearers of glad tidings and as forewarners. But those who have denied argue using falsehood in order to defeat the truth thereby, and they took[1]My signs and what they were warned of for a joke.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from present tense to past tense.

18:59.annotated: And those towns—We annihilated them when they committed injustices, and We set an appointment fortheir moment of annihilation[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem read it as: “. . . and We set an appointment for their annihilation .”

18:70.annotated: He said, “So if you<sup>sg </sup>follow me, then do not askme[1] about anything until I bring about a mention of it to you.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . then do not ever ask me about . . .”

18:71.annotated: So they both set out until, when they had boarded the ark, he holed it. He said, “Did you hole it so as to drown[1] its people? You have done something awful.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “Did you hole it so that its people would drown ?”

18:74.annotated: Then they both set out until, as soon as they encountered a boy, he killed him. He said, “Did you kill a sinless[1] self[2]which killed no one? Most surely, you have done something dreadful.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar and Roways read it as: “Did you kill an inherently sinless self . . .”
Literally, a ‘pure’ self.

18:77.annotated: So they both set out until, when they reached the people of a town, they asked them for food, but they refused to offer them hospitality. There they found a wall tending to collapse, so he repaired it. He said, “If you wanted, you could have charged[1] a reward for it.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “He said, ‘If you had wanted, you could have taken a reward for it.’”

18:86.annotated: until, when he had reached the setting of the sun, he found it setting in a murky[1] spring, and found a people in its vicinity. We said, “O Zul-Qarnayn, you may either punish or else treat them kindly.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Hafs and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . in a hot spring . . .”

18:88.annotated: But as for the one who has attained faith and has acted righteously, then for him is the excellent(reward) as repayment[1] , and we will speak to him with ease regarding our command.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer, Shuʻba and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . then for him is the repayment for the excellent (deed) , and we will . . .”

18:93.annotated: until, when he reached the point separating the two barriers, he found beside them a people who could barely comprehend[1] any word.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . who could barely make others comprehend any word.”

18:98.annotated: He said, “This is a mercy from my Lord; but when the promise of my Lord comes true, He will turn it into a flat surface[1] . And the promise of my Lord has always been true.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . turn it into rubble .”

18:99.annotated: And We left[1]them surging upon one another on that day, and the Trumpet was blown and We gathered them together.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

19:7.annotated: “O Zechariah, indeed, We give you glad tidings of a boy whose name is John; We have never made anyone similar to him[1]before.”

footnotes.text: At-Tabari mentioned that some exegetessaid that among the meanings of the Arabic word “sameyya” is‘someone with the same name’, so they considered him to be the first ever to be named as such.

19:9.annotated: He said, “Thus said your Lord, ‘It is easy for Me, and I[1] have certainly created youbefore when you were nothing.’”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “. . . and We have certainly created you . . .”

19:19.annotated: He said, “I am only a messenger of your Lord to grant[1] you a pure boy.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Warsh, Abu ʻAmr, Yaʻqub and Qaloun, in one of his narrations, read it as: “. . . of your Lord so that He may grant you . . .”

19:24.annotated: So he called her from beneath her[1] : “Be not sad; your Lord has made a stream beneath you.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer, Shuʻba and Roways read it as: “So the one beneath her called her :”

19:25.annotated: And shake the trunk of the palm tree towards you—it[1] will drop ripe datesupon you.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . it (masculine – referring to the trunk) will drop . . .” All others read it as: “. . . it (feminine – referring to the palm tree itself) will drop . . .”

19:28.annotated: O sister of Aaron[1], neither was your father an evil man, nor was your mother a harlot.”

footnotes.text: Aaron, to Jews, was an example of pious people who repent after sinning.

19:31.annotated: And He has made me blessed wherever I may be and has enjoined upon me prayer and purifying charity[1]so long as I live.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

19:34.annotated: That is Jesus, son of Mary—the word[1] of truth about which they are skeptical.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except Ibn ʻAmer, ʻAsem and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . son of Mary; (that is) the word of truth . . .”

19:40.annotated: Indeed, We—We alone—will inherit the earth and everyone on it, and to Us they are returned[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and to Us they return .”

19:51.annotated: And mention<sup>sg </sup>in the Scripture Moses. He was indeed a sincere, chosen one[1] , and he was a messenger(and) a prophet.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except ʻAsem, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “He was indeed sincere , and he was a messenger . . .”

19:55.annotated: And he used to command his family to prayer and purifying charity[1], and with his Lord he was always rendered pleased.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

19:58.annotated: Those are the ones whom Allah[1]blessed ofthe prophets from the offspring of Adam, and from those We[2]carried with Noah, and from the offspring of Abraham and Israel, and from those We guided and selected. Whenever the signs[3]of the All-Merciful<sup>b </sup>were recited to them, they would fall down prostrating and weeping.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

19:60.annotated: except for whoever repented and believed and acted righteously, for those shall enter[1] the Garden and shall not be dealt with unjustly in any way—

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Shuʻba, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . shall be entered into the Garden . . .”

19:64.annotated: “And we[1]do not descend except by the command of your<sup>sg </sup>Lord; to Him belongs whatever is before us and whatever is behind us and whatever is between them, and your Lord has never been forgetful.”

footnotes.text: Gabriel speaks about himself and about the angels.

19:66.annotated: And man says, “Can it be that when[1] I am dead,I willbe brought out alive?”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Zekwan, in one of his narrations, read it as: “. . . says, ‘When I am dead, will I be brought out alive?’”

19:72.annotated: Then We[1]deliver[2] those who were mindful(of God) and leave the unjust in it on their knees.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.
Qira’at: Al-Kesa’i and Yaʻqub read it as: “Then We save those who . . .”

19:73.annotated: And when Our signs[1]are read to them, evident, those who have denied say to those who have attained faith, “Which of the two groups is better in position[2] and fairerin company?”

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like‘verse’ in poetry or‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “‘Which of the two groups has a better dwelling place and is fairer in company?’”

19:75.annotated: Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Whoever has been in utter misguidance, may the All-Merciful fully extend for him[1].” Until, when they see what they were promised—either punishment or the Hour—then they will know who was in a worse position and weaker as an army.

footnotes.text: In wealth and time.

19:78.annotated: Has he viewed the hidden realm, or has he taken with the All-Merciful[1]a covenant?

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.
A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 2<sup>nd </sup>person..

20:2.annotated: We have not sent down the Recital[1]upon you<sup>sg </sup>for you to be wretched,

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’an which literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

20:5.annotated: the All-Merciful; on the Throne He settled[1].

footnotes.text: How He settled is beyond human understanding.

20:13.annotated: And I[1] have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “And We have indeed chosen you . . .”

20:32.annotated: and associatehim with me in my mission[1],

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . .my brother, (so that) I (can) strengthen myself with him 32 and (so that) I (can) associate him with me in my mission.”

20:39.annotated: ‘Throw him in the coffer then throw it into the waters, so that the waters will cast it onto the bank where an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will pick him up.’ For I bestowed upon you love from Me and so that you may be modeled[1] before My eye.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . and (I said): may you be modeled before My eye.”

20:52.annotated: He said, “Knowledge thereof is with my Lord in a record[1]; my Lord never goes astray nor does He forget.”

footnotes.text: Literally ‘scripture’.

20:53.annotated: (He is) the One Who has made the earth a cradle[1] for you<sup>pl </sup>and traced in it ways for you<sup>pl </sup>, and sent down from the sky water with which We[2]brought out pairs of diverse plants.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . a resting place for you . . .”
A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

20:58.annotated: We will most surely bring you sorcery like it; so make between us and you an appointment which we will[1] not break—neither us nor you—in a suitable place.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . we should not fail . . .”

20:63.annotated: They said, “These two are nothing but[1] sorcerers who want to evict you from your land with their sorcery and abolish your exemplary way of life.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs and Ibn Kathir read it as: “They said, ‘Most surely, these two are sorcerers …’”

20:64.annotated: So decide[1] your<sup>pl </sup>plot, then come, lined up(in ranks) ; and the one who gains the upper hand is surely bound to succeed today.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “So put together your plot . . .”

20:66.annotated: He said, “Rather, you<sup>pl </sup>cast.” And suddenly, their ropes and staffs were made to appear[1] to him, because of their sorcery, to be slithering.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Zekwan and Rouh read it as: “. . . their ropes and staffs appeared to him . . .”

20:69.annotated: And cast what is in your right hand—it will swallow[1] what they have crafted; what they have crafted is only a sorcerer’s[2] trickery, for the sorcerer will not succeed wherever he may go.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Zekwan read it as: “And cast what is in your right hand, to swallow . . .”
Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . a sorcery trickery . . .”

20:75.annotated: But whoever comes to Him as a believer, having done righteous deeds, then for those[1]are the highest degrees(of rank) :

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

20:77.annotated: And very truly, We revealed to Moses: “Journey by night with My servants and strike for them a dry road across the sea. You will not be[1] afraidof being overtaken nor apprehensive.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “Be not afraid of being overtaken . . .”

20:80.annotated: O Children of Israel, We[1] have surely saved youfrom your enemy, and have made an appointment with[2] you by the right side of Mount Tûr, and sent down to you manna and quails.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “I have surely saved you . . .”
Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and have promised you by the right . . .”

20:81.annotated: Eat of the good things We have provided for you<sup>pl </sup>, but do not exceed the limits in it lest you deserveMy wrath upon you, for the one upon whom My wrath is deserved[1] has surely fallen.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Al-Kesa’i read it as: “. . . lest My wrath descend upon you, for the one upon whom My wrath descends has surely fallen.”

20:87.annotated: They said, “We did not break our promise to you by our choice, but we were made to carry[1] burdens of the people’s ornaments, so we cast them and so did the Samiri cast.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr, Shuʻba, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i, Rouh and Khalaf read it as: “. . . but we carried burdens . . .”

20:88.annotated: So he brought out for them a calf—a mere body with a lowing sound. And they[1]said, “This is your god and the god of Moses, but he has forgotten.”

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

20:96.annotated: He said, “I perceived what they[1] did not perceive, so I grasped a handful from the messenger’s traces and I flung it away, and thus my soul prompted me.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . what you <sup>pl </sup>did not perceive . . .”

20:97.annotated: He said, “Be gone! For indeed your lot in this life is to say, ‘No touching’, and indeed you have an appointment that you will not be allowed to break[1] . And look at your god that you kept consecrating—we will certainly burn it up[2] then blow it away completely into the waters.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . that you will not break .”
Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . we will certainly burn it then blow it . . .”

20:101.annotated: abiding<sup>pl </sup>in it, and how bad their load became[1]on the Day of Resurrection—

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

20:102.annotated: the day when the Trumpet is blown[1] ! And We herd the criminals on that day, blue,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . when We blow the Trumpet!”

20:112.annotated: But whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, then he neither fears[1] injustice nor curtailment.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “. . . then he should neither fear injustice nor curtailment.”

20:113.annotated: And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic Recital[1], and We have diversified the warnings in it, that perhaps they would become mindful(of God) or it would bring about in them a remembrance.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

20:114.annotated: Most high above all is Allah, the True King. Do<sup>sg </sup>not be hasty with the Recital[1]before its revelation to you is concluded[2] , and say, “My Lord, increase me in knowledge.”

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.
Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . before We conclude its revelation to you . . .”

20:116.annotated: And recall when We said to the angels, “Prostrate yourselves to Adam.” So they prostrated themselves— but not Iblis[1]; he refused.

footnotes.text: Iblis is another name of Satan or Shaytan.

20:117.annotated: So We said, “O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your spouse. So do not let him get you<sup>dl </sup>out of the Garden, for then you<sup>sg </sup>will[1]suffer.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from dual to singular.

20:124.annotated: But whoever has disregarded My Reminder—for him is a miserable life, and We[1]will herd him on the Day of Resurrection blind.”

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

20:130.annotated: So bear patiently what they say and exalt your<sup>sg </sup>Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night exalt Him, and at the(two) ends of the day, that you may be well pleased[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “. . . that you may be rendered well pleased .”

20:131.annotated: And never extend your eyes towards what We have given some classes of them to enjoy—the splendor[1]of the Earlier Life—that We may test them thereby, for your Lord’s[2]provision is better and more lasting.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘flower’.
A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

21:4.annotated: He said[1] , “My Lord knows what is said in the heaven and the earth, for He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “Say <sup>sg </sup>. . .”

21:7.annotated: And never did We send before you<sup>sg </sup>but men to whom We reveal[1] , so ask the people of the Reminder if you<sup>pl </sup>do not know.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs read it as: “. . . to whom it is revealed , so ask . . .”

21:8.annotated: And never did We make them a mere body[1],(ones) who eat<sup>pl </sup>no food, for never were they immortal.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from plural to singular.

21:9.annotated: Then We fulfilled the promise to them, so We saved them together with whomever We will[1], and We annihilated the extremists.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from past tense to present tense.

21:24.annotated: Or have they taken apart from Him other gods? Say, “Bring your<sup>pl </sup>proof; this[1]is the reminder of those with me and the reminder of those before me.” Rather, most of them do not know the truth, so they disregard(it) .

footnotes.text: This Qur’an.

21:25.annotated: And never did We send any messenger before you<sup>sg </sup>but We[1] reveal[2]to him that: “There is no god but I, so worship<sup>pl </sup>Me.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . but it is revealed to him . . .”
Frequently the Qur’an speaks about the prophets using present tense; this should be pondered by the reader.

21:35.annotated: Every single self is bound to taste death, for We test you<sup>pl </sup>with evil and good as a means of trial, and to Us you are returned[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and to Us you return .”

21:45.annotated: Say, “Indeed, I am only warning you<sup>pl </sup>through revelation.” But the deafcannot hear[1] the call when they are being warned.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “But you cannot make the deaf hear . . .”

21:73.annotated: And We made them leaders, guiding by Our command, and We revealed to them(the command of) performing good works and establishing the prayer and bringing[1]the purifying charity[2], for of Us they were worshipers.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

21:75.annotated: And We entered him into Our mercy; He is[1]indeed one of the righteous.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an speaks about the prophets using present tense; this should be pondered by the reader.

21:80.annotated: And We taught him the making of shields for you<sup>pl </sup>, so that they may secure[1] youfrom your violence, so are you then appreciative?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba and Roways read it as: “. . . so that We may secure you . . .”All others except for Ibn ʻAmer, Hafs and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “so that He may secure you . . .”

21:81.annotated: And to Solomon the stormy wind[1] , blowing at his command towards the land that We had blessed. And We well knew of everything.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “winds ”.

21:87.annotated: And Jonah, when he went off angrily and he thought that We would not restrain him[1] . But then He cried out in the darkness(es) , “There is no god but You! Highly Exalted are You! Indeed, I have been one of the unjust!”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and he thought that he would not be restrained .”

21:88.annotated: So We responded to him and delivered him from stress, for thus We save the believers[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer and Shuʻba read it as: “. . . and thus the believers were saved .”

21:96.annotated: until, when Gog and Magog are opened[1] , and they swarm down from every mound,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . until, when Gog and Magog are opened wide . . .”

21:104.annotated: On the day when We fold the heaven[1] as the scribe rolls up scriptures[2] . Just as We began the first creation, We restore it—a promise from Us. We will indeed act.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “On the day when the heaven is folded as the scribe . . .”
Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “a scripture .”

21:105.annotated: And most surely We have written in the Book[1], after the Reminder[2], that the land will be inherited by My righteous servants.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: The Arabic word Zabourmeans ‘a book’ and it is the name of the book of David.
The Torah.

21:112.annotated: He said[1] , “My Lord, judge with justice.” “For our Lord is the All-Merciful, Whose help is sought against what you allege.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs read it as: “Say <sup>sg </sup>. . .”

22:5.annotated: O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection—We have indeed created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then from a clinging form, then from a lump of flesh,(partly) differentiated and(partly) undifferentiated, in order to clarify things for you. And We settle in the wombs whatever We will for a stated term, and then We bring you<sup>pl </sup>out as infants until you attain your full strength. And of you is one who is taken(at death) , and of you is one who is returned to the most abject age, so that he may not know anything after having known. And you<sup>sg </sup>see the land still, but when We send down water on it, it shakes and swells[1] and germinates all kinds of lovely plant.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . and becomes higher . . .”

22:9.annotated: turning aside in contempt, to make(others) stray[1] from the way of Allah; for him in the Earlier(Life) is disgrace, and on the Day of Resurrection We make him taste the punishment of burning:

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Roways read it as: “. . . to stray from the way of Allah . . .”

22:10.annotated: “That is for what your<sup>sg </sup>hands[1]have put forth, and because Allah is not a tyrant unto the servants.”

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 2<sup>nd </sup>person.

22:15.annotated: Whoever has been thinking that Allah will not support him[1]in the Earlier(Life) and the Hereafter—let him extend a means[2]to the sky, then cut(it) off, and see whether his plotting eliminates what enrages(him) .

footnotes.text: Referring to Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
Literally ‘rope’

22:16.annotated: And thus We sent it down as evident signs[1], for Allah guides whomever He wants.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

22:17.annotated: Indeed, those who have attained faith and those who have Judaized, and the Sabians[1]and the Christians and the Zoroastrians[2]and the Polytheists—indeed, Allah judges between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed, Allah is witness to everything.

footnotes.text: The Sabians were a monotheistic religious community.
Followers of an ancient Asian religion based on monotheism.

22:19.annotated: Here are two adversaries who have disputed regarding their Lord, so those who denied—garments of fire were tailored[1]for them, with scalding water pouring over their heads,

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the hereafter in past tense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

22:23.annotated: Indeed, Allah enters those who have attained faith and have done righteous deeds into Gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they are decorated with bracelets of goldand (with)[1]pearls, and their garments therein are of silk.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem, Nafieʻ, Yaʻqub and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . with bracelets of gold and(of) pearls . . .”

22:25.annotated: Indeed, those who have denied and bar(others) from the way of Allah and from the Inviolable Mosque, which We have designated for all mankind equally[1] ,(including) the one who consecrates himself therein and the visitor. And whoever wants any blasphemy unjustly therein—We will make him taste of a painful punishment.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs read it as: “. . . which We have designated for all mankind, equally for the one who consecrates himself therein and the visitor.”

22:28.annotated: that they may witness benefits for themselves and remember[1]the name of Allah during the known days[2]for providing them with livestock animals. So eat<sup>pl </sup>of it and feed the unfortunate poor.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used also means ‘mention’.
The days of Pilgrimage.

22:36.annotated: And We have made for you<sup>pl </sup>the(offering of) fleshy cattle among Allah’s rituals. In them is much good for you, so mention[1]Allah’s name upon them as they line up. Then when they have fallen to their sides[2], eat of them and feed the contented and the beggar. Thus We have subjected them to you, that you may give thanks.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used also means ‘remember’.
A metaphor for having been slaughtered.

22:38.annotated: Indeed, Allah defends[1] those who have attained faith. Indeed, Allah does not love every treacherous staunch denier.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “Indeed, Allah repels (harm) from those who . . .”

22:39.annotated: Permission has been granted[1] to those who are combated[2] , because they have been dealt with unjustly—and most surely Allah is Able to give them support:

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ, Abu ʻAmr, ʻAsem, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “He has granted permission to those . . .”
Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer, Hafs, and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . to those who combat . . .”

22:40.annotated: those who have been unjustifiably evicted from their homes merely for saying, “Our Lord is Allah.” And were it not that Allah repels people by means of others, monasteries and churches and synagogues and mosques—where the name of Allah is mentioned frequently—would have been utterly demolished[1] . And most surely, Allah will support whoever supports Him. Indeed, Allah is certainly All-Powerful, Almighty.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . would have been demolished .”

22:41.annotated: Those who, when We give them authority in the land, establish the prayer and bring[1]the purifying charity[2]and command to what is fair and forbid what is deplorable. And with Allah rests the outcome of all events.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

22:42.annotated: And if they disbelieve you<sup>sg </sup>—so before them the people of Noah andʻĀd[1]and Thamud[2](also) disbelieved,

footnotes.text: The pagan tribe of Prophet Hûd.
The pagan tribe of Prophet Salih.

22:45.annotated: So how many a town have We[1] annihilatedwhile it was unjust, so that it lies devastated upon its trellises, with an abandoned well and a lofty mansion?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . have I annihilated . . .”

22:47.annotated: And they urge you<sup>sg </sup>to hasten the punishment. But Allah will not break His promise. And indeed, a single day with your Lord is like a thousand years of what you<sup>pl </sup>count[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . of what they count .”

22:51.annotated: But those who strove against Our signs[1]attempting to challenge[2] (the believers) —those are the fellows of purgatory.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . attempting to thwart . . .”

22:62.annotated: That is because Allah is the Truth, and because whatever they[1] call uponapart from Him is falsehood, and because Allah is the All-High, the Supreme.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʻAmer, Shuʻba and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . whatever you call upon . . .”

22:70.annotated: Have you<sup>sg </sup>not come to know that Allah knows whatever is in the heaven and the earth? Indeed, that is in a record[1]; indeed, that is easy for Allah.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘scripture’.

22:71.annotated: Yet they worship, apart from Allah, things for which He sent down[1] no authority and what they have no knowledge of. And for the unjust<sup>pl </sup>there is no supporter.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . things for which Hebestowed no authorityfrom on high . . .”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . whom they call upon . . .”

So establish the prayer and bring[1]the purifying charity[2]and hold fast to Allah. He is your Patron, so what an excellent Patron and what an excellent Supporter!

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . their prayer . . .”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer and Shuʻba read it as: “bone ”.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . in livestock: It gives you to drink . . .”

footnotes.text: That was the sign to embark the ship.
Qira’at: All except for Hafs read it as: “‘…of each (male and female) kind, one couple…’”

footnotes.text: Follow one another into destruction.

23:51.annotated: “O messengers, eat of the good foods and do righteousness; indeed, I am All-Knowing of what you do[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . of what you do. And (know) that this community . . .”

footnotes.text: Literally ‘scripture’.

23:67.annotated: in arrogance regarding it, conversing by night(about it) ,(yet) deserting[1] it[2] .”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ read it as: “. . . conversing by night (about it), (yet) blaspheming .”

23:85.annotated: They will say, “To Allah.” Say<sup>sg </sup>, “Will you never remember[1] ?”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “Say<sup>sg </sup>, ‘Will you not constantly remember ?’”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “They will say, ‘Allah .’”

23:92.annotated: the Knower[1] of the hidden realm and the manifest. So Most High is He, far above what they associate(as gods with Him) .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Shuʻba, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i, Abu Jaʻfar and Khalaf read it as: “. . . describe. (He is) the Knower of . . .”

23:106.annotated: They said[1], “Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us, and we were a people astray.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

23:111.annotated: Today I have indeed rewarded them for what they endured patiently, forit[1]is they who are the triumphant ones.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “. . . patiently. Indeed, it is they . . .”

23:112.annotated: He said[1] , “How long did you remain on earth in terms of number of years?”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Hamza and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “Say <sup>sg </sup>, ‘How long…’”

23:114.annotated: He said[1] , “You<sup>pl </sup>remained but for a little while, if you only knew.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza and Al-Kesa’i read it as: “Say <sup>sg </sup>, ‘You remained…’”

23:115.annotated: Did you<sup>pl </sup>think that We had created you in vain, and that to Us you would not be returned[1] ?”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i, Yaʻqub and Khalaf read it as: “. . . you would not return ?”

24:1.annotated: A surah[1]that We have sent down and ordained[2] and sent down in it evident signs[3], that you may remind yourselves[4] .

footnotes.text: Each portion of the Qur’an is called a ‘surah’, which is sometimes translated as ‘chapter’.
Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . and did ordain . . .”

Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . that you may constantly remember .”

24:2.annotated: The fornicating woman and the fornicating man—whip each one of them a hundred lashes and let no compassion towards them keep you<sup>pl </sup>from carrying out Allah’s religion, if you(truly) believe in Allah and the Last Day, and let their punishment be witnessed by a group[1]of believers.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is the same as that translated as ‘faction’.

24:6.annotated: And those who accuse their own spouses but have no witnesses except themselves, then let the testimony of one of them be four oaths[1] by Allah that he is surely of the truthful.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . then the testimony of one of them (is binding)—four oaths by Allah . . .”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . may Allah’s curse be upon him . . .”

24:9.annotated: while[1] the fifth is: may Allah’s wrath indeed beupon her if he is of the truthful.

footnotes.text: According to Al-Alousi and other exegetes, this sentence is left open-ended in order to magnify the predicate and leave it to the reader’s imagination.

24:12.annotated: If only when you<sup>pl </sup>heard it, the believing men and the believing women had thought well of themselves[1]and said, “This is an evident fabrication!”

footnotes.text: The Qur’an used the term ‘themselves’ rather than ‘each other’ to make the believerssympathizewith one another by considering any defamation of one as defamation of all.

24:20.annotated: And were it not for Allah’s grace upon you<sup>pl </sup>, and His mercy, and that Allah is Compassionate, Bestowing of mercy. . .[1]

footnotes.text: According to Al-Alousi and other exegetes, this sentence is left open-ended in order to magnify the predicate and leave it to the reader’s imagination.

24:26.annotated: Nasty[1]ones are for nasty men, and nasty men are for nasty ones, and good ones are for good men, and good men are for good ones. Those are acquitted of what they say; for them is forgiveness and a noble provision.

footnotes.text: The words ‘nasty’ and ‘good’ are mentioned in feminine form and may refer either to ‘nasty women’ and ‘good women’ or to ‘nasty words and ‘good words’.

24:30.annotated: Tell<sup>sg </sup>the believing men to restrain their sight(s) [1]and to preserve their private parts; that is purer for them. Indeed, Allah is All-Aware of what they do.

footnotes.text: Mentioned in plural form in Arabic, denoted by (s) in English for grammatical reasons.

24:33.annotated: And let those who do not find the means to marry remain chaste until Allah enriches them from His grace. And if any of those whom you<sup>pl </sup>rightfully possess desire an(emancipation) agreement, write an agreement with them if you recognize some good in them, and give them of Allah’s wealth which He has given you. And do not compel your maids to prostitution, seeking the materials of the Earlier(Life) , if they want to remain chaste. But should anyone compel them—then after their compulsion, Allah is indeed Oft-Forgiving[1], Bestowing of mercy.

footnotes.text: Of such maids.

24:34.annotated: And We have most surely sent down to you<sup>pl </sup>clarifying[1] signs and a parable from those who passed on before you[2], and an admonition for the ones who were mindful(of God) .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Ibn ʻAmer, Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . clarified signs . . .”
Referring to the story of the slander of Yusuf.

24:35.annotated: Allah is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The parable of His light is as a niche wherein is a lamp; the lamp is in a glass; the glass is like a glittering planet, kindled[1] from a blessed tree—an olive tree—neither eastern nor western. Its oil would almost illuminate even if no fire were to touch it. Light upon light. Allah guides to His light whomever He wills. Thus Allah sets forth parables for mankind. For Allah is All-Knowing of everything.

footnotes.text: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar, Yaʻqub, Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Hafs read “kindled” in masculine form referring to the lamp being kindled from the oil of a blessed tree. All others read it in feminine form referring to the glass being kindled.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, and Shuʻba read it as: “He is highly exalted therein, mornings and before sunset — 37men whom . . .”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “And He bestows from on high, from the sky—from mountains . . .”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “And Allah is the Creator of every treading creature . . .”

footnotes.text: The Prophet (peace be upon him).

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba read it as: “. . . as those before them were made successors (of others) . . .”

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer and Hamza read it as: “Those who have denied should never think that they can thwart . . .”

24:58.annotated: O you who have attained faith, let those whom you rightfully possess and those of you who have not reached puberty seek your permission[1] (befor e entering) onthree occasions: before the dawn prayer and at noon when you lay aside your clothes and after the evening prayer—three occasions of privacy for you. footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Shuʻba, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . seek your permission (before entering). Three occasions . . .”

24:63.annotated: Do not make the calling of the Messenger among yourselves like your calling of one another. Allah certainly knows those[1]among you who slip away, concealed by others. So let those who oppose his command beware, lest a trial afflict them or a painful punishment afflict them.

footnotes.text: The hypocrites.

24:64.annotated: Undoubtedly, to Allah does belong whatever is in the heavens and the earth; surely, He knows your<sup>pl </sup>condition. And on the day they are returned[1] to Him, He informs them of what they did. For Allah is All-Knowing of everything.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . they return to Him . . .”

25:1.annotated: Supremely Blessed be the One Who bestowed the Criterion from on high upon His servant, to be a warner[1]to all realms.

footnotes.text: The Arabic text can imply either the Prophet (peace be upon him) as a warner, or the Criterion as a warning.

25:8.annotated: or if a treasure were to be cast to him, or if he had a garden from which he eats[1] .” And the unjust ones said, “You<sup>pl </sup>are only following a bewitched man.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “‘…from which we eat .’”

Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . then We say . . .”

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

25:19.annotated: Thus they[1]have certainly disbelieved you<sup>pl </sup>regarding what you say, so you[2] can neither avoid(punishment) nor get any support. And whoever of you commits injustice, We will make him taste a supreme punishment.

Qira’at: All except for Hafs read it as: “. . . so they can neither avoid (punishment) . . .”

25:22.annotated: On the day when they see the angels—no glad tidings for the criminals on that day, and they[1]say, “an insurmountable separator[2].”

footnotes.text: The angels.
From bliss.

25:23.annotated: And We proceeded[1]to the work they had done and turned them into scattered dust.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the hereafter in pasttense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “. . . and We send down the angels in streams.”

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’an which means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

25:38.annotated: and(for) ʻĀd[1]and Thamûd[2]and the fellows of Al-Russ[3]and many generations in between.

The pagan tribe of Prophet Salih.
At-Tabari mentioned that some exegetes said thatAl-Russ was a huge water pit.

footnotes.text: The city inhabited by the people of Lot.

25:48.annotated: And it is He Who sent the winds[1] as heralds of glad tidings[2] ahead of His mercy. And We[3]sent down from the sky pure water

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “wind ”.

Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . as revivers ahead of His mercy”.All except for ʻAsem, Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . as a revival ahead of His mercy”.
A grammatical shift from 3<sup>rd </sup>person to 1<sup>st </sup>person.

25:50.annotated: And most surely We have circulated it among them, that they may constantly remember[1] , yet most of mankind refused anything but constant denial.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . that they may remember . . .”

25:52.annotated: So do not obey<sup>sg </sup>the deniers, but strive against them with it[1]a supreme striving.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an.

25:60.annotated: And when it is said to them, “Prostrate yourselves to the All-Merciful,” they say, “And what is the All-Merciful? Shall we prostrate ourselves to what you command[1] us?” And it increases their aversion.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . in it lamps and . . .”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza and Khalaf read it as: “. . . wants to remember or wants to . . .”

25:73.annotated: And they are those who, when reminded of the signs[1]of their Lord, do not fall before them deaf and blind.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ, Ibn kathir, Ibn ʻAmer, Hafs, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . our offspring . . .”

25:75.annotated: Those are awarded the Chamber(in Heaven) for their patience, and are received[1] therein with greetings and peace,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . and will encounter therein greetings and peace . . .”
