footnotes.text: This night is known as the night ofQadr (Surah number 97), in the month of Ramadan.

44:7.annotated: (from the) Lord[1] of the heavens and the earth and what is between them, if you<sup>pl </sup>(can ever) believe with certitude.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . the All-Knowing. 7(He is the) Lord of the . . .”

44:17.annotated: And surely before them We tested the people of Pharaoh when a noble messenger[1]came to them,

footnotes.text: Prophet Musa, or Moses.

44:37.annotated: Are they better, or the people of Tubbaʻ[1]and those before them? We annihilated them; indeed, they were criminals.

footnotes.text: Tubbaʻis the name of a Yemenite tribal chief.

44:42.annotated: except for one upon whom Allah has had[1]mercy; indeed, He is the Almighty, the Bestower of mercy.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in past tense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.
Trees in Hell which produce hot, bitter, rotten fruit.

44:45.annotated: like molten brass boiling[1] in the bellies

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Ibn Kathir and Hafs read it as: “Indeed, the tree of Zaqqumis the food of the sinful one— 45like molten brass— boiling in the bellies . . .”

44:49.annotated: “Taste<sup>sg </sup>! You[1] —indeed you—are the mighty, the noble[2].

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Al-Kesa’i read it as: “Taste <sup>sg </sup>, that you —indeed you—are the . . .”
This is said in sarcasm.

44:50.annotated: Indeed, this is what you<sup>pl </sup>were[1]skeptical about.”

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

44:56.annotated: Therein they do not taste death beyond the first death, and He[1]shielded them from the punishment of Hell—

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 1<sup>st </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

44:58.annotated: Thus have We made it[1]easy through your<sup>sg </sup>tongue, that they may remind themselves.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an.

45:5.annotated: And the alternation of night and day, and the provision Allah has sent down from the sky, with which He has revived the earth after its death, and the shifting of the winds[1] are signs for people who reason.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “wind ”.

45:6.annotated: Those are Allah’s signs[1]which We read to you<sup>sg </sup>in truth. So in which discourse, after Allah and His signs, will they[2] believe?

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.
Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Hafs, Abu Jaʻfar and Rouh read it as: “. . . will you <sup>pl </sup>believe ?”

45:8.annotated: who hears Allah’s signs<sup>b </sup>being read to him, yet he persists arrogantly, as though he did not hear them. So give<sup>sg </sup>him glad tidings[1]of a painful punishment.

footnotes.text: This is said in sarcasm.

45:9.annotated: And when he learns something of Our signs, he takes them in mockery; for those[1]is a demeaning punishment.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

45:11.annotated: This is guidance, but those who have denied their Lord’s signs—for them is a painful punishment of torment[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Ibn Kathir, Hafs and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . for them is a punishment of a painful torment .”

45:14.annotated: Tell<sup>sg </sup>those who have attained faith to forgive those who do not expect the Days of Allah, that He may repay[1] peoplefor what they used to earn.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . that We may repay people . . .”Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . that people may be repaid . . .”

45:15.annotated: Whoever acts righteously does so to his own benefit, while whoever commits evil does so to his own detriment, then to your<sup>pl </sup>Lord you are returned[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . then to your Lord you <sup>pl </sup>return .”

45:21.annotated: Or do those who have perpetrated evil deeds assume that We will make them asequal to those who have attained faith and have done righteous deeds, whether[1] in their life or their death? Miserableis their judgment!

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “Or do those who have perpetrated evil deeds assume that We will make them as those who have attained faith and have done righteous deeds? Equal is their life or their death; miserable is their judgment!”

45:23.annotated: Have you<sup>sg </sup>seen the one who has taken his own whim as his god, and Allah has misguided him despite his knowledge, and has sealed his hearing and his heart, and has placed a veil over his sight? Who will guide him after Allah? Will you not remind[1] yourselves?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “Will you not constantly remind yourselves?”

45:25.annotated: And when Our signs[1]are recited to them, evident, their only argument is to say, “Bring back our forefathers, if you<sup>pl </sup>are truthful.”

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

45:28.annotated: And you<sup>sg </sup>see every community kneeling; every[1] community iscalled to its Scripture: “Today you<sup>pl </sup>are being repaid for what you used to do:

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “And you<sup>sg </sup>see every community kneeling, every community being called . . .”

45:32.annotated: And when it is said, “Indeed, the promise of Allah is true”—while of the Hour[1] there is no doubt—you<sup>pl </sup>say, “We do not know what the Hour is; we are only making a guess; we are not certain.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “And when it is said, “Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and of the Hour there is no doubt . . .” you <sup>pl </sup> say . . .”

45:33.annotated: And the evils of what they had done became evident to them[1], and they became surrounded by what they used to ridicule.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in past tense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

45:35.annotated: That is because you<sup>pl </sup>dealt with Allah’s signs[1]with ridicule, and the Earlier Life deceived you.” So today they are not brought[2] outof it, and they are not allowed to make amends.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God
Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “So today they do not come out of it.”

46:12.annotated: And before it was the Scripture of Moses, a guide and a mercy. And this is a confirming Scripture in the Arabic tongue, that it may warn[1] those who have done injustice, and as glad tidings for those who excel in doing good.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Al-Bazzi, Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . that you may warn those . . .”

46:15.annotated: And We have enjoined upon man excelling in showing kindness[1] to his parents; his mother carried him with difficulty and delivered him with difficulty; his carriage and weaning are thirty months. Until, when he has attained his full strength and has reached forty years, he says, “Lord, enable me to appreciate the blessings with which You have blessed me and my parents, and to do righteousness that well pleases You, and grant me righteousness in my offspring. Indeed, I have repented to You, and indeed I am of the Muslims[2].”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . upon man kindness to . . .”
The Arabic word used is Muslimeenwhich means those who willingly submit to God, regardless of which prophet they followed.

46:16.annotated: Those are the ones from whom We accept the best of what they have done and whose misdeeds We overlook[1] ;(they are) among the fellows of the Garden(of Paradise) —the promise of truth which they had been promised.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . from whomthe best of what they have done is bound to be accepted and whose misdeeds are bound to be overlooked . . .”

46:18.annotated: Those are the ones upon whom the sentence is justified, among the communities that have passed away before them of unseen beings[1]and humans; they were indeed losers.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is jinnwhich are unseen beings that are accountable for their actions.

46:19.annotated: And for all, there are degrees according to what they have done, and that He may render[1] to them in full(the reward) for their deeds, and they will not be dealt with unjustly.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Hisham, ʻAsem and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and that We may render . . .”

46:21.annotated: And recall the brother of ʻĀd[1]when he warned his people at the dunes—and warnings had passed away before him and after him: “Worship none but Allah; I fear for you<sup>pl </sup>the punishment of a great day.”

footnotes.text: Prophet Hûd who was sent to the people of ʻĀd.

46:23.annotated: He said, “Indeed, all knowledge is only with Allah, and I proclaim[1] to youwhat I have been sent with, but I see you are an ignorant people.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . and I compile and proclaim to you . . .”

46:25.annotated: destroying everything by the command of its Lord.” And when the morning came upon them, nothing could be seen[1] except their residences. Thus We repay the criminal people.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for ʻAsem, Hamza, Yaʻqub and Khalaf read it as: “. . . you <sup>sg </sup>could see nothing except . . .”

46:26.annotated: And surely We had empowered them in the same way as We empowered you<sup>pl </sup>and We gave them hearing, and sight(s) [1], and burning hearts. But neither their hearing, nor their sight(s) , nor their burning hearts availed them in any way. That is because they used to repudiate the signs[2]of Allah, and so they became surrounded by what they used to ridicule.

footnotes.text: Mentioned in plural form in Arabic, denoted by (s) in English for grammatical reasons.

The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like‘verse’ in poetry or‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

46:28.annotated: Why then did those whom they worshiped as means of nearness to Allah not support them? Rather, they abandoned[1]them. It was their lie, a fabrication of their own making.

footnotes.text: Literally “they strayed from them.”

46:29.annotated: And recall when We dispatched towards you<sup>sg </sup>several unseen beings[1]to listen to the Recital[2]. When they came in its presence, they said, “Listen<sup>pl </sup>quietly!” Then, when it was concluded, they turned to their people, forewarning them.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is jinnwhich are unseen beings that are accountable for their actions.
The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

46:33.annotated: Have they not seen that Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth and was never tired by creating them, is capable[1] ofreviving the dead? Yes indeed; He is indeed powerful over all things.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . by creating them, can revive the dead?”

47:4.annotated: Thus, when you<sup>pl </sup>encounter those who have denied, strike at their necks. Then when you have subjugated them, bind them firmly[1]. Then either release them by grace or by ransom until war lays down its burdens. Had Allah willed, He could have defeated them Himself, but He thus tests some of you by means of others. As for those who were killed[2] in the way of Allah, He will not let their deeds go to waste.

footnotes.text: i.e. Take them as captives.
Qira’at: All except for Abu ʻAmr, Hafs and Yaʻqub read it as: “As for those who combated in the way of Allah . . .”

47:13.annotated: And how many a town was more powerful than your town[1]which evicted you<sup>sg </sup>? We annihilated them, and there was no helper for them.

footnotes.text: Addressing Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) about the town which evicted him (Makkah).

47:14.annotated: Is someone who relies on evident proof from his Lord like someone the evil of whose work was adorned for him? And they[1]followed their own whims.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

47:15.annotated: The likeness of the Garden(of Paradise) that the mindful<sup>pl </sup>(of God) have been promised: rivers of water, notstaling[1]; and rivers of milk whose taste has not changed; and rivers of wine, a delight for those who drink; and rivers of honey, clarified and pure. And they have therein of all products and forgiveness from their Lord.(How can this be) compared to the fate of those abiding in the Fire and were given, for drink, scalding water, so that it tore their bowels?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “. . . rivers of water, never staling . . .”

47:16.annotated: And among them is one who listens to you<sup>sg </sup>, but when they[1]depart from your presence, they say to those given knowledge, “What did he say just now?” Those are the ones whose hearts Allah has sealed, and they followed their own whims.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural. The difference between this shift and the one in sign number 14 should be pondered by the reader.

47:20.annotated: And those who have attained faith say, “If only a surah[1]was sent down.” Yet when a decisive surah is sent down and combat is mentioned in it, you<sup>sg </sup>see those in whose hearts is sickness looking at you with the look of someone fainting at death. Yet worthier of them would be

footnotes.text: Each portion of the Qur’an is called a ‘surah’, which is sometimes translated as ‘chapter’.

47:22.annotated: Would you<sup>pl </sup>then, in case you became in charge[1] , spread corruption in the earth and sever[2] your family ties[3]?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Roways read it as: “. . . in case you were made in charge , spread corruption . . .”
Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and cut your family ties?
Literally “sever your wombs”.

47:23.annotated: Those are the ones whom Allah has cursed, so He made them deaf and blinded their sight(s) [1].

footnotes.text: Mentioned in plural form in Arabic, denoted by (s) in English for grammatical reasons.

47:24.annotated: Will they not ponder the Recital[1], or are there locks upon their hearts?

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means recital or recitation.

47:25.annotated: Indeed, those who turned on their heels after guidance became evident to them—Satan has enticed themand has filled[1] themwith false hopes.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “Satan has enticed them. Thus they were filled with false hopes.”Yaʻqub read it as: “Satan has enticed them. Thus I filled them with false hopes.”

47:26.annotated: That is because they said to those who hated what Allah had bestowed from on high, “We will obey you in certain matters.” But Allah knows their secret exchanges[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . their secrets .”

47:31.annotated: And We[1] will certainly test you<sup>pl </sup>until We knowthose of you who strive and those who are steadfastly patient, and(until We) test[2] your reactions.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba read it as: “And He will certainly test you <sup>pl </sup> until He knows those of you who strive and those who are steadfastly patient, and (until He) tests your reactions.”
Qira’at: Roways read it as: “. . . those who are steadfastly patient. And We will test your reactions.”

48:9.annotated: that you<sup>pl </sup>may believe[1] in Allah and His Messenger, and rally to Him and honor Him and highly exalt Him morning and evening.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . .that they may believe in Allah . . .”

48:10.annotated: Indeed, those who pledge allegiance to you<sup>sg </sup>are actually pledging allegiance to Allah: the hand of Allah is over their hands. So whoever reneges in fact reneges to his own detriment. And whoever fulfills what he has covenanted with Allah, then He[1] will grant hima great reward.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafie’, Ibn Kathir, Abu Ja’far and Rouh read it as: “. . . then We will grant him a great reward.”

48:15.annotated: Those who lagged behind will say when you<sup>pl </sup>depart to collect the gains[1], “Let us follow you.” They want to change the Speech[2] of Allah. Say<sup>sg </sup>, “You will not follow us; Allah has said so before.” Then they will say, “Rather, you<sup>pl </sup>envy us.” In fact, they have not comprehended except a little.

footnotes.text: The spoils of war.
Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . the Words of Allah.”

48:17.annotated: There is no blame on the blind, nor any blame on the lame, nor any blame on the sick. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger—He[1] will enter himinto Gardens beneath which rivers flow. But whoever turns away—Hewill punish himwith a painful punishment.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . We will enter him ...We will punish him . . .”

48:24.annotated: And it is He who withheld their hands from you<sup>pl </sup>and your hands from them in the valley of Makkah after giving you advantage over them, for Allah has always been All-Seeing of what you[1] do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . what they do .”

48:25.annotated: It is they who have denied, and barred you<sup>pl </sup>from the Inviolable Mosque, and prevented the offering from reaching its destination. And were it not for(the presence among them of) some faithful men and some faithful women whom you did not know of and whom you would have hurt, thus incurring dishonor unknowingly on their account . . .[1]—that Allah may enter into His mercy whomever He wills. If they had been apart, We would have punished those of them who denied with a painful punishment.

footnotes.text: This sentence is left open-ended; according to Al-Qurtubi and other exegetes the predicate is elided but can be understood as: “I would not have prevented you from retaliating.”

48:26.annotated: Those who denied filled their hearts with chauvinism—the chauvinism of paganignorance[1]. But Allah sent His tranquility down upon His Messenger and upon the believers and imposed on them the word of mindfulness(of God) of which they were most worthy and deserving, for Allah has always been All-Knowing of everything.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is jahiliyahwhich is derived from jahlor ‘ignorance’ and refers to the pre-Islamic phase of paganism.

49:6.annotated: O you who have attained faith, if an ungodly person brings you any news, investigate[1] (the matter) , lest you harm a people out of ignorance and thus become regretful for what you have done.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . brings you any news, ascertain (the truth) . . .”

49:10.annotated: Indeed, all the believers are but brothers, so reconcile between your<sup>pl </sup>two brothers[1] and be mindful of Allah, that you may receive mercy.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . so reconcile between your <sup>pl </sup>brothers . . .”

49:11.annotated: O you who have attained faith, no people shall ridicule other people, for they may be better than them. Nor shall any women ridicule other women, for they may be better than them. Nor shall you defame yourselves[1], nor shall you insult one another by nicknames. What a miserable label ungodliness is after attaining faith! And whoever has not repented—then those[2]are the unjust.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an used the term ‘yourselves’ rather than ‘each other’ to make the believers sympathize with one another byregarding any defamation of one as defamation of all.
A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

49:18.annotated: Allah knows the hidden realm of the heavens and the earth, for Allah is All-Seeing of what you[1] do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “. . . what they do .”
The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.
That which is sworn is omitted so that the reader may ponder.

50:3.annotated: Can it be that when we have died and become dust . . .[1]? This is a far-fetched return.”

footnotes.text: This sentence is left open-ended; according to Al-Alousi and other exegetes the predicate is elided but can be understood as: “. . . that we shall be brought back again?”

50:4.annotated: We have already known what the earth consumes of them, and with Us is a constantly preserving record[1].

footnotes.text: Literally ‘scripture’.

50:17.annotated: As the two receptors[1]receive(him) , one on the right and one on the left, constantly seated.

footnotes.text: Two angels who receive everyone’s words and deeds during his/her life and record them.

50:20.annotated: And the Trumpet was blown[1]: “That is the Day of the Threat.”

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in past tense, this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

50:21.annotated: And every soul came forward, accompanied by a driver and a witness[1].

footnotes.text: Two angels: one drives the person to the place of assembly and the other is a witness to all his/her deeds.

50:23.annotated: And His comrade[1]said, “This is what I have ready with me.”

footnotes.text: According to Ibn ʻAshour, some exegetes said that this comrade is an angel, and others said it is his intimate friend in life, while others said it is his devil which used to whisper to him.

50:30.annotated: On the day when We say[1] to Hell, “Are you full?” And it says, “Are there any more?”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ and Shuʻba read it as: “. . . when He says to Hell . . .”

50:32.annotated: This is what you<sup>pl </sup>are promised[1] —for every constant preserver who often turns to God,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir read it as: “This is what they are promised . . .”

50:38.annotated: And surely We created the heavens and the earth and what is between them in six days[1], and never were We touched by any fatigue.

footnotes.text: Six equal intervals of time, which may be six heavenly days, each of them being 1000 earthly years long (see 22:47).

50:40.annotated: And highly exalt<sup>sg </sup>Him with praise in the night and after[1] prostrations.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Hamza, Abu Jaʻfar and Khalaf read it as: “. . . and at the ends of prostrations.”

50:44.annotated: The day the earth ruptures[1] open from above them, letting them rush out; that is an easy exodus for Us.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . the earth vigorously ruptures open . . .”

50:45.annotated: We know better what they say, and you<sup>sg </sup>are not a compeller over them, so remind by the Recital[1]whoever fears My warning.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.
The first four signs are interpreted as the winds spreading the clouds, carrying them, moving them and distributing them.
Different opinions about the judgment.
Literally ‘May the conjecturers be killed’.

51:24.annotated: Has the story of Abraham’s[1] honored guests reached you<sup>sg </sup>?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham in one of his narrations read it as: “Abraham ”.

51:41.annotated: And(likewise) in(the people of) ʻĀd[1]—We sent against them the Barren Wind,

footnotes.text: The pagan tribe of Prophet Hûd.

51:43.annotated: And(likewise) in(the people of) Thamûd[1]—they were told, “Enjoy yourselves for a while.”

footnotes.text: The pagan tribe of Prophet Salih.

51:44.annotated: But they defied the command of their Lord, so the Lightningstruck[1]them as they looked on,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Al-Kesa’i read it as: “. . . so the strike of lightning struck them as they . . .”

51:46.annotated: And(recall) before that, the people[1] of Noah—indeed, they were a defiantly disobedient people.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “And (likewise) before that, (in) the people of Noah . . .”

51:49.annotated: And We created all things in pairs, that you may remind[1] yourselves.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . that you<sup>pl </sup>may constantly remember .”

51:56.annotated: And I did not create the unseen beings[1]and humans but to worship Me.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is jinnwhich are unseen beings that are accountable for their actions.

52:21.annotated: And those who attained faith and whose offspring[1] followed themin faith—We have united[2]them with theiroffspring[3] , and We have not deprived them of anything of their work; every person is in pledge for what(deeds) he has earned.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . and whose offspring(s) followed them . . .”Abu ʻAmr read it as: “And those who attained faith and whom We followed (with) their offspring(s) in faith . . .”
Frequently, the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in past tense; this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.
Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Abu ʻAmr, Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . their offspring(s) . . .”

52:26.annotated: They said, “When we were still with our families[1]we used to live in fear[2],

footnotes.text: During their life on earth.
Fear of falling into sin.

52:28.annotated: Indeed, before this we used to pray to Him; indeed ,[1] He is the Fulfiller of promises, the Bestower of mercy.”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Al-Kesa’i and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . to Him, for He is . . .”

52:30.annotated: Or do they say, “A poet[1]for whom we await a calamity of time”?

footnotes.text: Some pagans claimed that Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was a poet who authored the Qur’an.

52:45.annotated: So leave<sup>sg </sup>them until they meet[1] their day in which they are stunned—

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . until they encounter their . . .”

53:5.annotated: taught to him by the extremely powerful,[1]

footnotes.text: Referring to Angel Gabriel.

53:11.annotated: The burning heart did not lie[1] aboutwhat it saw.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hisham and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “The burning heart did not disbelieve what it saw.”

53:12.annotated: Will you<sup>pl </sup>enter into controversies[1] with himdespitewhat he sees?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i, Khalaf and Yaʻqub read it as: “Will you<sup>pl </sup>discredit him despite what he sees?”

53:14.annotated: at the Lote-tree of the Extremity[1],

footnotes.text: The Lote-tree of the Extremity is a spot above the seven firmaments; none has ever crossed it, and it is where Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) saw Angel Gabriel in the heavens at the night of his ascendance (Mi’raj).

53:20.annotated: And Manāt[1], the third one, the other?

footnotes.text: Al-Lāt, Al-ʻUzzaand Manātwere names of three goddesses in Arabia.

53:21.annotated: Are you<sup>pl </sup>to have the males and He the females[1]?

footnotes.text: Though pagan Arabs considered having daughters to be shameful, they attributed it to God, so the Qur’an is debating them according to their own logic.

53:32.annotated: Those who avoid the gravest[1] of sinsand obscenities—except for minor lapses—your<sup>sg </sup>Lord is of vast forgiveness. He knows better about you<sup>pl </sup>, ever since He initiated you from the earth, and ever since you were fetuses in your mothers’ bellies. So do not acclaim your own purity—He knows better who is mindful(of Him) .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “Those who avoid the grave kind of sin and . . .”

53:37.annotated: and of Abraham[1] who fulfilled(conveying the commandments) :

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham read it as: “Abraham ”.

53:45.annotated: and that He created the two spouses[1]—the male and the female,

footnotes.text: The Arabic word, zawjayn,can also mean ‘two kinds’ or ‘two types’.

53:49.annotated: and that it is He Who is the Lord of Sirius[1];

footnotes.text: Sirius was a star worshiped by pagan Arabs.

53:50.annotated: and that He annihilated ancient ʻĀd[1]

footnotes.text: The pagan tribe of Prophet Hûd.
The pagan tribe of Prophet Salih.

53:52.annotated: and the people of Noah before that; indeed, they were more unjust and more exceeding of all limits[1].

footnotes.text: Comparing their injustices and atrocities to those of the people of Quraysh, the tribe of Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).

53:53.annotated: And He brought down the Ruined Cities[1]

footnotes.text: Where the people of Prophet Lot lived.

54:11.annotated: So We opened[1] the gates of the sky with water pouring down,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “So We widely opened the . . .”

54:17.annotated: And most surely We have made the Recital[1]easy for remembrance, so is there anyone to remind himself?

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

54:18.annotated: ʻĀd[1]disbelieved, so how were My punishment and My warnings!

footnotes.text: The pagan tribe of Prophet Hûd.
The pagan tribe of Prophet Salih.

54:26.annotated: They[1] will knowtomorrow who the wicked sheer liar is.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer and Hamza read it as: “You <sup>pl </sup>will know tomorrow . . .”

54:28.annotated: And inform<sup>sg </sup>them that the water is to be shared between them[1]; each one should drink in turn.

footnotes.text: The water is to be shared between them and the she-camel.

54:32.annotated: And most surely We made the Recital[1]easy for remembrance, so is there anyone to remind himself?

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

54:36.annotated: And most surely he[1]had warned them of Our onslaught, but they entered into controversies about the warnings.

footnotes.text: Prophet Lot.

54:48.annotated: The day when they are dragged upon their faces into the Fire: “Taste the touch of Saqar[1].”

footnotes.text: Saqaris one of the names which the Qur’an gave to the fire of Hell.
The Arabic word used is Qur’an which literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

55:6.annotated: and the plants[1]and the trees prostrate themselves.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is najmwhich also means ‘star’; notice the suitability of the term which connects what is before it with what is after it.

55:12.annotated: and grains[1] in the blades, and fragrant plants.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . palm trees. 12 And (He created) grains in the blades, and (he created) fragrant plants .”Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . and (grains of) fragrant plants .”

55:13.annotated: So which of your Lord’s marvels do you<sup>dl </sup>disbelieve in[1]?

footnotes.text: The Qur’an is addressing the two types of responsible creatures: humans and jinn.

55:15.annotated: and created the unseen being[1]from a smokeless flame of fire.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is jānn(the singular of jinn), which is an unseen being that is accountable for its actions.

55:19.annotated: He merged the two waters[1], converging together;

footnotes.text: Either the fresh water of rivers and the salty water of seas, or the waters of two different oceans.

55:22.annotated: From them come out[1] pearls and corals.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “From them are brought out pearls and corals .”

55:24.annotated: His are the running ships, whose sails are raised[1] in the sea like banners[2].

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza and Shuʻba in one of his narrations read it as: “His are the running ships that raise their sails in the sea like banners.”
The Arabic word used is Aʻlāmwhich also means ‘tall mountains’.

55:26.annotated: Everyone upon it[1]is bound to perish,

footnotes.text: The earth.

55:31.annotated: We[1] will attendto you<sup>pl </sup>, O two huge communities<sup>c </sup>.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Yaʻqub read it as: “He will attend to you . . .”

55:33.annotated: O society of unseen beings and humans, if you<sup>pl </sup>can penetrate the bounds of the heavens and the earth then go ahead and penetrate; you will never penetrate except with authority[1].

footnotes.text: The Qur’anic style involves leaving part of the meaning to be deduced by the listener; Ar-Rāzi and other exegetes said that this may mean ‘except with authority from God’, or ‘except with authority that you do not have’.

55:35.annotated: Flares of fire, and brass[1] , will be sent upon you<sup>dl </sup>, and you will not find help.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Rouh read it as: “Flares of fire and (of) brass . . .”

55:39.annotated: On that day neither any human nor unseen being[1]is asked about his misdeeds.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is jānn(the singular of jinn), which is an unseen being that is accountable for its actions.

55:78.annotated: Supremely Blessed be the Name of your<sup>sg </sup>Lord,the Possessor[1] ofmajesty and nobility.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . the Name of your<sup>sg </sup>Lord, which possesses majesty and nobility.”

56:19.annotated: causing them neither headache nor intoxication[1] ,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except ʻAsem, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . causing them no headache , and they are not intoxicated . . .”

56:22.annotated: And(in it are) spouses[1] with lovely wide eyes,

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . and meat of any bird they may desire, 22and (leaning on) spouses with . . .”
The Arabic word used for refreshing is kareemwhich literally means ‘noble’.

56:47.annotated: and they used to say, “Can it be that when we have died and become dust and bones—can it be that[1] we will really be resurrected?

footnotes.text: Nafieʻ, Al-Kesa’i, Abu Jaʻfar and Yaʻqub read it as: “Can it be that when we have died and become dust and bones we will really be . . .”
Qira’at: Qaloun, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . really be resurrected? 48Or our ancient forefathers ?”

56:52.annotated: will certainly be eating from the trees of Zaqqum[1]

footnotes.text: Trees in Hell which produce hot, bitter, rotten fruit.

56:62.annotated: And you<sup>pl </sup>have certainly known the first formation; if only you would remind[1] yourselves!

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except Hafs, Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . if only you would constantly remember !”
Qira’at: Shuʻba read it as: “Can it be that we will really be in debt? Rather . . .”

56:75.annotated: I swear by the locations[1] of the stars—

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “. . . by the location of the stars . . .”

56:77.annotated: It is indeed a Noble Recital[1]

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

56:83.annotated: So when it[1]has reached the throat,

footnotes.text: The soul of a dying person.

56:89.annotated: then serenity[1] andfragrant plants and a Garden of Bliss.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Roways read it as: “. . . then a soul with fragrant plants and a Garden of bliss.”

57:4.annotated: It is He Who created the heavens and the earth in six days[1]then settled over the Throne. He knows what penetrates the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the sky and what ascends to it, for He is with you<sup>pl </sup>wherever you may be. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.

footnotes.text: Six equal intervals of time, which may be six heavenly days, each of them being 1000 earthly years long; (see 22:47).

57:5.annotated: To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, ʻAsem and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . all matters return .”

57:8.annotated: And what is the matter with you<sup>pl </sup>that you do not believe in Allah when the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord—when He has taken[1] your pledge[2] — if you are believers?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . your Lord—when your pledge has been taken . . .”
God took a pledge from all humans in a pre-earthly existence; see (Verse 7:172).

57:9.annotated: It is He who bestows[1] upon His servant evident signs from on highto bring you<sup>pl </sup>out of darkness(es) into light. And towards you Allah is truly Compassionate, Bestowing of mercy.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Yaʻqub read it as: “It is He who sends down upon His servant evident signs to bring . . .”

57:10.annotated: And why is it that you<sup>pl </sup>do not spend in the way of Allah when to Allah belongs the inheritance of the heavens and the earth? Not equal among you are those who spent before the conquest and combated; those are higher in degrees(of rank) than those who spent afterwards and combated, yet to each[1] Allah has promisedthe best(reward) , and Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . and combated. Yet each—Allah has promised (him) . . .”

57:13.annotated: On the day when the hypocritical men and hypocritical women say to those who believed, “Wait for[1] us so that we may borrow from your light.” They were told[2]: “Go back behind you and seek light.” Then a wall with a door was raised between them: within it is mercy and outside of it is punishment.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza read it as: “Reprieve us so that . . .”
Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in past tense, this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.

57:14.annotated: They[1]call to them[2], “Were we not with you?” They said, “Yes, but you tempted yourselves and waited and doubted and became deceived by fancies until the command of Allah arrived, and the deceiver[3]deceived you regarding Allah.

footnotes.text: The hypocrites.
The believers.
Satan.

57:16.annotated: Is it not time for those who have attained faith: that their hearts should become reverent towards Allah’s Reminder and to that which came down[1] of the truth, and not be[2] like those who were given the Scripture previously, but for whom time became prolonged so that their hearts hardened, and many of them are defiantly disobedient?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except for Nafieʻ and Hafs read it as: “. . . to that which He bestowed from on high of the truth . . .”
Qira’at: Roways read it as: “. . . of the truth. And do not be like those . . .”

57:18.annotated: Indeed, charitable men and charitable women[1] who have loaned Allah a good loan—it will be multiplied for them, and for them is a noble reward.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Shuʻba read it as: “Indeed, men who believe and women who believe, who have loaned . . .”

57:19.annotated: And as for those who have attained faith in Allah and His messengers—those are the unwavering believers and the witnesses[1]who will come as witnesses with their Lord; for them is their reward and their light. But as for those who denied and rejected Our signs—those are the fellows of purgatory.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is shuhada’, which literally means ‘witnesses’ and is usually used to describe martyrs.

57:22.annotated: No calamity occurs on earth or among yourselves but it is already written in a Record[1]before We make it— indeed, that is easy for Allah—

footnotes.text: Literally ‘scripture’.

57:23.annotated: so that you<sup>pl </sup>do not grieve over what you have missed nor exult over what He has given[1] you. And Allah does not love every self-admiring boaster—

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . nor exult over what has come to you.”

57:24.annotated: those who are miserly and command mankind to miserliness. And whoever turns away—indeed, it is Allah who is[1] the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . indeed, Allah is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy.”

57:26.annotated: And We certainly sent Noah and Abraham[1] and established Prophethood and Scripture among their offspring, so some of them are rightly guided, while many of them are defiantly disobedient.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham read it as: “Abraham ”.

58:7.annotated: Have you<sup>sg </sup>not seen that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth? There is no secret conversation between three but He is their fourth, nor between five but He is their sixth, nor less than that nor more[1] but He is with them wherever they may be. Then on the Day of Resurrection He will inform them of what they did; indeed, Allah is All-Knowing of everything.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “. . . nor less than that, nor (is there) more but He is with them . . .”

58:8.annotated: Have you<sup>sg </sup>not seen those who were prohibited from conversing secretly but then revert to what they were prohibited from? They converse secretly[1] in sin and hostility and(in) disobedience to the Messenger. And when they come to you<sup>sg </sup>they greet you with a greeting that Allah never greeted you with, and they say within themselves, “Why does Allah not punish us for what we say?” Hell is enough for them; they will roast in it—so what a miserable destiny!

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza and Roways read it as: “. . . they converse with one another secretly in sin . . .”

58:9.annotated: O you who have attained faith, when you converse secretly, do not converse secretly[1] in sin and hostility and(in) disobedience to the Messenger, but converse in virtue and mindfulness(of God) , and be mindful of Allah to Whom you will be herded.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Roways read it as: “. . . do not converse with one another secretly in sin . . .”

58:10.annotated: Indeed,(malicious) private conversations are from Satan, that those who have attained faith may be sad[1] . But he cannot harm them at all except by Allah’s leave. And in Allah let the believers place their trust.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ read it as: “. . . that he may make those who have attained faith sad .”

58:11.annotated: O you who have attained faith, when you are told, “Make room for one another in assemblies[1] ,” then make room so that Allah makes room for you. And when you are told, “Arise,” then arise. Allah elevates by degrees those of you who have attained faith and those given knowledge. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: All except ʻAsem read it as: “. . . in the assembly .”

58:13.annotated: Are you<sup>pl </sup>reluctant to give donations before your private conversation? If you do not do so and Allah pardons you, then establish the prayer and bring[1]the purifying charity[2]and obey Allah and His Messenger. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an always uses verb ‘to bring’ rather than verb ‘to give’ in association with charity; this should be pondered by the reader.
The Arabic word used is zakāt, which denotes purification and growth.

58:20.annotated: Indeed, those who oppose Allah and His Messenger are among the most humiliated[1].

footnotes.text: They shall be humiliated in the Hereafter.

59:2.annotated: It is He who evicted those who denied among the People of the Scripture from their homes at the first exodus[1]. You<sup>pl </sup>did not think they would depart, and they thought their fortresses would protect them from Allah, but Allah came at them from where they never expected and threw terror into their hearts. They[2]wreck[3] their houses with their own hands and by the hands of the believers. So take a lesson, O you who are endowed with sight(s) .

footnotes.text: The Jewish tribe of Banu al-Nadirwas besieged by the Muslims for trying to assassinate the Prophet (peace be upon him). An arbiter ruled that its members had to leave Madinah; some of them left to Khaybarwhile the rest left to the Levant.
A grammatical shift from past tense to present tense, which serves to create a vivid portrait of past events.
Qira’at: Abu ʻAmr read it as: “They vigorously wreck their houses . . .”

59:7.annotated: Whatever Allah has turned over to His Messenger from the people of the towns, then that is for Allah and for the Messenger and for the relative and the orphans and the destitute<sup>pl </sup>and to the traveler in need, so that it does notcirculate exclusively[1] between the wealthy among you. And whatever the Messenger brings you—accept it, and whatever he forbids you—abstain from it. And be mindful of Allah; indeed, Allah is stern in retribution.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Abu Jaʻfar and Hisham read it as: “. . . so that a closed circuit is not created between the wealthy among you.”

59:8.annotated: (It is) for the poor immigrants[1]who were evicted from their homes and their possessions, seeking grace from Allah, and(His) good pleasure, and supporting Allah and His Messenger— those are the sincere.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is muhajereen, which refers to the Muslims of Makkahwho were forced to flee as refugees from their homes to Madinahwhere they were welcomed.

59:9.annotated: And(for) those who,before them,had settled in the homeland and(adopted) the faith—theylove those who emigrated to them and find no need in their chests for what has been brought to them, and they give them priority over themselves even if they themselves are needy. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his(inner) self—then it is those[1]who are the successful.

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from singular to plural.

59:14.annotated: They do not combat you<sup>pl </sup>all together except from fortified strongholds or from behind walls[1] . Their hostility towards each other is severe. You<sup>sg </sup>would think them united, but their hearts are diverse; that is because they are people who do not reason.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn Kathir and Abu ʻAmr read it as: “. . . or from behind a wall .”

59:17.annotated: So the consequence for both of them was[1]that they are[2]in the Fire, abiding therein, and such is the repayment of the unjust.

footnotes.text: Frequently the Qur’an addresses the events of the Hereafter in past tense, this grammatical shift should be pondered by the reader.
A grammatical shift to present tense, which serves to create a vivid portrait of future events.

59:21.annotated: Had We sent this Recital[1]down upon a mountain, you<sup>sg </sup>would have seen it(trembling) in reverence, crumbling in awe of Allah. And these parables We set forth for mankind, that they may reflect.

footnotes.text: The Arabic word used is Qur’anwhich literally means ‘recital’ or ‘recitation’.

60:3.annotated: Neither your relatives[1]nor your children will benefit you; on the Day of Resurrection Hewill decide[2] betweenyou, for Allah is All-Seeing of what you do.

footnotes.text: Literally ‘your wombs’.

Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . on the Day of Resurrection a decision will be made between you . . .” Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . on the Day of Resurrection youwill be separated . . .” All except for Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr, Abu Jaʻfar, Ibn ʻAmer, ʻAsem and Yaʻqub read it as: “on the Day of Resurrection He will separate you . . .”

60:4.annotated: Surely, there has always been an excellent role model for you<sup>pl </sup>in Abraham[1] and those with him, when they said to their people, “We disown you and what you worship apart from Allah. We have disbelieved[2]in you, and enmity and hatred have surfaced between us and you forever until you believe in Allah alone.” Except for the words of Abraham to his father, “I will ask forgiveness for you, though I cannot protect you from Allah.” “Our Lord, in You we have placed our trust, and to You we have turned penitent, for to You is the destiny.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Though pronounced in Arabic as Ibrahim, Hisham read it as: “Abraham ”.
Literally ‘denied’.

60:9.annotated: Rather, Allah forbids you<sup>pl </sup>from[1]those who combated you over religion and evicted you from your homes and backed up(your enemies) in your eviction. And whoever takes them as guardians—those are the unjust.

footnotes.text: The prohibition is from befriending them or forming an alliance with them.

60:10.annotated: O you who have attained faith, when believing women come to you immigrating, test them; Allah knows better about their faith. And if you<sup>pl </sup>find them to be faithful, do not send them back to the deniers; they are not lawful for them[1]nor are they lawful for them[2]. But give them what they have spent[3]. And no sin is committed by you if you marry them, provided you give them their compensation<sup>g </sup>. And do not hold on to ties with unbelieving women, but demand what you have spent and let them demand what they have spent. This is Allah’s judgment—He judges among you, for Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.

footnotes.text: As wives.
As husbands.
The dowries paid to the brides.

61:6.annotated: And recall when Jesus, son of Mary, said, “O Children of Israel, I am Allah’s Messenger to you, confirming what preceded me of the Torah and a bearer of glad tidings of a messenger who comes after me, whose name is Ahmad.” Yet when he came to them with evident proofs, they said, “This is evident sorcery[1] .”

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Hamza, Al-Kesa’i and Khalaf read it as: “‘This is an evident sorcerer .’”

61:10.annotated: O you who have attained faith, shall I inform you of a bargain that will save[1] you from a painful punishment?

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Ibn ʻAmer read it as: “. . . that will deliver you from . . .”

61:14.annotated: O you who have attained faith, be the supporters[1] ofAllah as Jesus, son of Mary, said to the disciples, “Who are my supporters towards Allah?” The disciples said, “We are the supporters of Allah.” Then a faction of the Children of Israel attained faith while another faction denied it, and We aided those who had attained faith against their enemy, so they came to prevail.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn Kathir, Abu ʻAmr and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . be supporters for Allah . . .”

62:2.annotated: It is He who sent among the gentiles[1]a messenger from among themselves, reading His signs[2]to them and purifying them and teaching them the Scripture and wisdom—although they were indeed in evident misguidance before that—

footnotes.text: Literally ‘the unlettered’.

The Arabic word used isayat(singularayah). Ayahmeans ‘sign’ or ‘proof’. It is also used to denote the unit of text in the Qur’an,like ‘verse’ in poetry or ‘sentence’ in prose.Each such unit isconsidered a ‘sign’from God.

62:3.annotated: and(to) others of them who have not yet joined them[1]. And He is the Almighty, the All-Wise.

footnotes.text: Non-Arab believers.

62:11.annotated: Yet whenever they[1]come across a bargain or distraction they scramble towards it and leave you<sup>sg </sup>standing. Say, “What is with Allah is better than(any) distraction or bargain, and Allah is the Best of providers.”

footnotes.text: A grammatical shift from 2<sup>nd </sup>person to 3<sup>rd </sup>person.

63:5.annotated: And when it is said to them, “Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you,” they keep turning[1] their heads aside and you<sup>sg </sup>see them turning away while acting arrogantly.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Nafieʻ and Rouh read it as: “. . . they turn their heads . . .”

63:11.annotated: But Allah will not delay a soul when its time has come, for Allah is All-Aware of what you<sup>pl </sup>do[1] .

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Shuʻba read it as: “. . . what they do .”

64:8.annotated: So have faith in Allah and His Messenger and the Light[1]which We have sent down. For Allah is All-Aware of what you do.

footnotes.text: The Qur’an.

64:9.annotated: The day when He[1] gathersyou<sup>pl </sup>for the Day of Gathering—that is the Day of Mutual Loss and Gain. And whoever attains faith in Allah and acts righteously, He[2] will remit his evil deeds and Hewill enter himinto Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever; that is the great triumph.

footnotes.text: Qira’at: Yaʻqub read it as: “The day when We gather you . . .”
Qira’at: Nafieʻ, Ibn ʻAmer and Abu Jaʻfar read it as: “. . . We will remit his evil deeds and We will enter him into . . .”

65:1.annotated: O Prophet, when you<sup>pl </sup>divorce[1]women, then divorce them at a time when their(waiting) period can properly start, and calculate the period carefully. And be mindful of Allah, your<sup>pl </sup>Lord. Do not evict them from their houses nor shall they depart, unless they have committed an evident obscenity[2] . Those are the limits of Allah, and whoever oversteps Allah’s limits, then he has surely been unjust to himself. You<sup>sg </sup>never know—Allah may afterwards bring about a new matter.

footnotes.text: It is obvious from the masculine plural pronoun that the Qur’an is addressing men.
